# GA Forum: full rankings

Source: https://ga-forum.com. Generated 2026-11-18. Vendors can pay for more visibility; how that works is explained in our disclosure, linked above every ranking. No commission is earned on clicks or purchases, and we do not work as an affiliate.

## Best 2D Game Engines in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-2d-game-engines
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A 2D game engine is software for making games drawn in flat planes: sprite animation, tilemaps, collision, scene editing and export to devices. Some are full editors with visual tools, others are code libraries for the browser. This ranking covers both and compares editor tools, export targets and license terms published by each vendor.

1. GameMaker (https://gamemaker.io/): Built only for 2D, with Xbox, PlayStation and Switch among its homepage targets and a free tier for prototypes, which settles the top spot for sprite-driven work. Pricing: A free tier with no credit card; Professional adds commercial release and Enterprise adds console release, neither with a price on the homepage. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Console release sits behind the Enterprise tier, and neither paid tier shows a price on the homepage, so budgeting needs a sales or store visit.
2. Godot (https://godotengine.org/): Free, open source and equipped with a dedicated 2D engine, so a studio pays nothing and keeps full control of the editor and its source. Pricing: No charge. The homepage calls it free and open source and makes no further pricing claim; it does not name the license in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Console export is not built in: the homepage says consoles run through third-party publishers.
3. Phaser (https://github.com/phaserjs/phaser): A code-first framework tuned for the browser, with GPU tilemap and sprite layers that suit large 2D scenes. Pricing: Free under the MIT license, per the official repository page. Free option: Open source. Falls short: There is no visual editor in the facts we found, so level design relies on external tools. iOS, Android and Steam builds depend on third-party wrappers rather than a first-party exporter.
4. Defold (https://defold.com/): A free, all-in-one engine whose editor bundles tilemap and particle tools, with a broad platform list and no royalties. Pricing: Described as free forever with no up-front cost, no licensing cost, no royalties and no runtime fee, under a source-available license. Free option: Free. Falls short: The license is described as source available, not open source, so check the terms if you plan to fork.
5. GDevelop (https://gdevelop.io/): A no-code event editor that turns game logic into rules, with one-click exports to web, Android, Steam and iOS. Pricing: The engine is described as open source, with paid Silver and Gold plans whose prices are not shown in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: iOS publishing sits on the higher paid plan, and neither plan shows a price in the page text.
6. LOVE (https://love2d.org/): A minimal Lua framework whose license allows any commercial use, with a track record that includes Balatro. Pricing: Free, with commercial use allowed without limitations under the zlib/libpng license. Free option: Open source. Falls short: There is no editor, scene designer or tilemap tool in the facts, so everything beyond drawing needs libraries or custom code. iOS is delivered as source, not a ready build.
7. Solar2D (https://solar2d.com/): A Lua engine with a fast simulator and mobile-first heritage, free and royalty-free under the MIT license. Pricing: Free under the MIT license; the homepage promises no hidden fees, charges or royalties. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Funding relies on user sponsorship, a thinner base than a foundation or company.
8. Cocos Creator (https://cocos.com/): A full toolchain engine for 2D and 3D with strong partner names, held back by a homepage that gives no license or price. Pricing: The homepage states no price or license; it shows a download button and a link to a store. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No license, price or specific platform list is stated on the homepage, so a studio cannot judge cost or reach from it.
9. KAPLAY (https://kaplayjs.com/): A friendly TypeScript game library with an online playground, suited to short projects that live on the web. Pricing: Free and open source, with optional donations through Open Collective and Cafecito; the license name is not in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Its scope is the web only, as far as the page says, with no native or console path.
10. Excalibur.js (https://excaliburjs.com/): A TypeScript engine with a permissive BSD license and clear documentation, and an optional paid support route. Pricing: Free under the BSD 2 Clause license; a Premium Support page is linked with no price shown. Free option: Open source. Falls short: No Premium Support price is shown.
11. Stencyl (https://stencyl.com/): A block-based builder with a scene designer and monetization hooks, but no published pricing and an aging homepage. Pricing: A Pricing section is linked but the homepage states no plan names or amounts. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices or plan names are published, so a team cannot size the spend.
12. Buildbox (https://buildbox.com/): A no-code tool for people with no technical background, ranked last because the facts show no price, platform list or feature detail. Pricing: Not stated on the page; a Get Buildbox link leads to a download page with no price or trial shown. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The page states no price, no free trial, no platform list and no feature list, so almost nothing can be verified before download.

## Best 3D Game Engines for Small Studios in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-3d-game-engines-for-small-studios
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A 3D game engine is a toolkit for building games with depth: it renders scenes, handles physics, animation and audio, and exports to devices. For small studios, the relevant questions are cost, royalty and source access. This ranking covers engines for desktop, console and mobile, and web 3D tools, using terms published by each vendor.

1. Unity (https://unity.com/): Leads on reach: more than 25 platforms and a services stack, though its licensing figures are not on the homepage. Pricing: The homepage offers a free start and a plans page, but prints neither figures nor tier names. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Licensing is the page's weak spot: the homepage links to plans and pricing but shows no numbers, and the royalty or fee structure is the main test for this ranking.
2. Godot (https://godotengine.org/): No fee, readable source and a foundation behind it, which makes the cost side of a small-studio plan very easy. Pricing: The vendor calls it free and open source and states nothing else about price; the license is not named in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The homepage describes its 3D as simple, which is an honest limit for studios chasing film-grade visuals.
3. Flax Engine (https://flaxengine.com/): Full source code and three scripting options for small and larger teams, offset by terms that live on a separate page. Pricing: The homepage advertises full source code and links a Licensing page; no license name, royalty or price is in the page text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Neither the license name, royalty terms nor prices appear in the page text, and no platform list is given on the homepage.
4. CryEngine (https://cryengine.com/): The only entry with an explicit royalty rate and exemption stated on its homepage, plus full source access. Pricing: Free to use, 5% royalty once you ship, with the first $5K of annual revenue per project royalty-free. Free option: Free. Falls short: The platform line names PC, Xbox, PlayStation and Oculus, without mobile or Switch, so a phone or handheld plan needs another engine.
5. Bevy (https://bevy.org/): A code-first Rust engine with permissive licensing, suited to programmers more than to artists. Pricing: Free, with no contracts, license fees or sales cuts; optional donor tiers run from $25 to $6,000 per month. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The facts show no visual editor in the feature list, so artists and designers depend on programmers for scene work.
6. Stride (https://stride3d.net/): A C# engine with a complete editor toolchain and MIT terms, but a platform list limited to desktop and VR. Pricing: Free; the editor and runtime source are MIT licensed, and an Open Collective donation link is offered. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Only desktop and VR are named as targets, which leaves phones, consoles and the web unconfirmed.
7. O3DE (https://o3de.org/): Open-source engine run through the Open 3D Foundation, strong on modular design, thin on pricing and license detail. Pricing: The homepage states no price and promotes donations and membership; the license is not named in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: No pricing, software license name or specific platform list appears on the homepage.
8. Fyrox (https://fyrox.rs/): A Rust engine since 2019 whose homepage reveals little about license, price, platforms or tools. Pricing: The homepage states no price; it links to a sponsor page with no pricing detail. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No license, price, platform or feature information is shown on the homepage, so there is nothing here to verify.
9. Babylon.js (https://www.babylonjs.com/): A web rendering engine with WebGPU support and native runtimes, but no stated license or price on its homepage. Pricing: The homepage states neither a price nor a license. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage states no license or price, which is the main criterion of this ranking, so check the repository.
10. Wonderland Engine (https://wonderlandengine.com/): A web-first XR engine with a visual editor and a free start, aimed at browser delivery more than store games. Pricing: Teams can start with a free license and a Get started free option; plan names and prices are not in the page text. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Plan names and prices are not published in the page text, so commercial costs stay unknown until you open the pricing page.
11. Three.js (https://threejs.org/): A JavaScript library whose homepage lists no license, price or platform facts, so it ranks low on terms. Pricing: The homepage states neither price nor license. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: License, price and platforms are not stated on the homepage, and no editor, asset pipeline or game framework is part of the facts.
12. Needle Engine (https://needle.tools/): Ships scenes from Unity or Blender to the browser, but commercial use needs a paid tier whose price is not listed. Pricing: Free for personal projects; commercial use requires Go Pro, with no figures on the homepage. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Commercial studios must pay for Go Pro, and the homepage shows no price.

## Best AI NPC and Dialogue Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-ai-npc-and-dialogue-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

An AI NPC and dialogue platform lets a non-player character speak, answer players and remember context, using language models, speech synthesis and animation, or classic branching scripts. The category covers conversational engines such as Convai, authoring languages such as ink and Yarn Spinner, voice services, and tools that generate surrounding assets.

1. Convai (https://convai.com/): Closest to a finished NPC product here: characters, engine plugins and a credit meter in one place, with a free tier to start on. Pricing: Billing is credit-based: every conversation turn, connected session and processed file draws from the plan's credit balance, and the pricing page mentions free-tier access for developers. Free option: Free. Falls short: Plan amounts sit behind a JavaScript pricing page that we could not read, so cost per player cannot be checked here.
2. NVIDIA ACE (https://developer.nvidia.com/ace-for-games): The deepest technical stack of the group, spanning speech, language and face animation, though it asks you to assemble the parts yourself. Pricing: No price is shown on the ACE for Games page, which offers Get Started and Notify Me buttons instead. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: This is a toolkit, not a character editor, so design, memory and dialogue tooling are yours to build.
3. Inworld (https://inworld.ai/): Published, metered prices and a voice stack make it easy to model costs, but the pitch has moved from game characters to consumer voice. Pricing: The On-Demand plan costs USD 0 to start and bills per use (TTS-2 at USD 25 per 1M characters, open-model LLM inference from USD 0.07 per 1M tokens); a Creator plan is USD 25 per month. Free option: Free. Falls short: The homepage no longer leads with game characters, so NPC-specific tooling such as personalities or in-engine plugins is not visible in what we read.
4. ElevenLabs (https://elevenlabs.io/): Not an NPC brain, but the broadest published voice and sound tooling, with a free tier and prices anyone can read. Pricing: Free tier with 10k credits per month; Starter is $1 for the first month then $6; Creator $22; Pro $99; Scale $299; Business $990; Enterprise is custom. Free option: Free. Falls short: Credits are consumed per generation, so a game that voices lines live for many players needs a volume quote beyond the self-serve tiers.
5. Dialogue System for Unity (https://www.pixelcrushers.com/dialogue-system/): The practical bridge between traditional branching dialogue and language models, provided your project already lives in Unity. Pricing: No price appears on the opened pages; an evaluation version can be downloaded and the asset is sold through the Unity Asset Store. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Everything runs inside Unity, so Godot and Unreal projects are out.
6. Yarn Spinner (https://yarnspinner.dev/): Best when writers need to own the dialogue: plain-text scripts, three engines, and a long list of shipped games. Pricing: Free and paid versions exist for each engine, and the pages we opened show no price figures. Free option: Free. Falls short: It produces authored, deterministic dialogue.
7. ink (https://www.inklestudios.com/ink/): Zero cost and proven by inkle's own games, but strictly an authoring language rather than an AI character platform. Pricing: Free: ink, the Inky editor and the Unity plugin are released under the MIT license. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Unity gets the official plugin; Unreal support comes from The Chinese Room's Inkpot container rather than inkle.
8. articy:draft X (https://www.articy.com/en/): Strong organization for large branching narratives, with engine exports, though it plans dialogue rather than generating it. Pricing: A free version exists; Multi-User and Single-User licenses are sold on a pricing page whose amounts did not appear in the text we read. Free option: Free. Falls short: It runs only on Windows and macOS.
9. Scenario (https://www.scenario.com/): Useful beside an NPC system for portraits and assets, though it generates content, not conversations. Pricing: Starter is $15 per month, Pro $45 and Max $75, with Enterprise on custom pricing; 50 free daily credits need no card, and annual billing saves 33 percent. Free option: Free. Falls short: It does not handle speech, personalities or conversation state, so it cannot make an NPC talk.
10. Layer (https://layer.ai/): Wide model choice and no seat fees, yet tier amounts are not readable and the output is assets, not NPC speech. Pricing: Usage-based with unlimited members at $0 per seat; tier amounts were not in the opened text, and the pricing page links to a calculator and to sales. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Because pricing is usage-based and the tier numbers sit behind a calculator, you cannot compare cost with other entries here.
11. Ludo.ai (https://ludo.ai/): An inexpensive way to fill a prototype with art and sound, listed last because it creates assets rather than dialogue. Pricing: Indie is $15 per month billed annually ($180 a year, 3,000 credits), Pro $35 per month annually, Studio $300 per month annually; start free with 30 credits. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Nothing on the opened pages covers dialogue, voice acting or character behavior.

## Best Clip and Highlight Editors for Streamers in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-clip-and-highlight-editors-for-streamers
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A clip and highlight editor for streamers finds or records the best moments of a broadcast or play session and turns them into short, often vertical, videos for TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. Some tools capture clips while you play, others use AI on a finished stream, and others are general editors for polishing the result.

1. StreamLadder (https://www.streamladder.com/): Starts from a Twitch, YouTube or Kick stream and ends with vertical clips for short-video apps, with prices published on the page. Pricing: Free to start; paid plans from $15 to $39 a month for Starter, Creator and Pro, with a 7-day free trial on any paid plan. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The free plan exists but the facts do not say what it limits, so the cap on clips has to be read on the pricing page.
2. Eklipse (https://eklipse.gg): Turns Twitch, YouTube and Kick streams into captioned vertical clips and schedules them to TikTok, Reels and Shorts. Pricing: A free feature set plus paid plans compared on the pricing page (amounts not captured from the page). Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Paid plan amounts were not captured from the pricing page we read, so the real monthly cost needs checking directly.
3. Medal (https://medal.tv/): Free on PC to record, edit and share gaming clips, which makes it the cheapest start for a player who clips mid-match. Pricing: Free to download and use on PC, per the homepage meta description. Free option: Free. Falls short: Medal is PC-only according to the listing, and the facts do not describe any stream-to-vertical conversion.
4. OpusClip (https://www.opus.pro/): Cuts long videos into short clips and offers a free trial that needs no credit card. Pricing: Starter and Pro plans with monthly or yearly billing; free trial without a credit card (amounts not captured from the page). Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The pricing amounts were not captured from the page we read.
5. Vizard (https://vizard.ai): A web clipper with a free tier of 60 credits per month and a yearly price marked 50 percent off. Pricing: Free plan at $0 with 60 credits a month; paid plans with credit packs billed monthly or yearly (yearly shown with a 50 percent discount). Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Credits are consumed per job, so a streamer cutting many hours of VODs may burn through 60 credits fast.
6. Outplayed (https://outplayed.tv/): Records your best plays automatically while you play and adds a video editor and performance tracking. Pricing: Free and Premium tiers. Premium removes ads and unlocks premium features; prices were not on the opened page. Free option: Free. Falls short: Premium prices were not on the page we opened, and the free tier carries ads.
7. CapCut (https://www.capcut.com): A full editor with templates and effects, and Free, Pro, Ultra and Teams plans, rather than a gaming clipper. Pricing: Free, Pro, Ultra and Teams plans, with monthly or yearly billing (amounts not captured from the page). Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Plan amounts were not captured, and the product is not stream-aware, so you must bring in your own footage.
8. NVIDIA App (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/nvidia-app/): Lists ShadowPlay and the Broadcast App beside driver updates, so capture is already on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU. Pricing: The download page shows no price; ShadowPlay and the Broadcast App are listed as features of the app. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It only makes sense with NVIDIA hardware, and the page opened shows no clip editor or vertical export.
9. AMD Software Adrenalin (https://www.amd.com/en/products/software/adrenalin.html): AMD's own application for driver updates, game stats and capturing in-game moments on its graphics products. Pricing: No price is shown on the AMD page opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The listing shows no price and no editing features, so every clip needs another tool before it can be posted.
10. OBS Studio (https://obsproject.com/): Free and open source recording and streaming software that feeds the rest of these tools with source video. Pricing: Free and open source software. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The facts do not list auto-highlighting, an editor or vertical export, so you need a second tool such as StreamLadder or Eklipse to produce clips from OBS recordings.

## Best Cloud Gaming Services in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-cloud-gaming-services
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Cloud gaming services run a game on a remote server and send the video to your phone, TV, browser or laptop while your controller input travels back. They differ in what you play: a catalog the service licenses, games you already own in other stores, or a full rented Windows PC.

1. GeForce NOW (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/): It streams purchases from Steam, Epic, GOG and more, with a top tier built on newer RTX servers, so a big library pays off immediately. Pricing: Paid Performance and Ultimate memberships; amounts were not readable on the membership page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Membership prices were not in the readable text of the membership page, and the device list was not captured.
2. Xbox Cloud Gaming (https://play.xbox.com/): Cloud play comes bundled with Game Pass, so subscribers get hundreds of games on consoles and PCs without extra hardware or a second bill. Pricing: Included in Xbox Game Pass; the page gives no amount in readable text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The play.xbox.com page returned almost no text, so we could not check cloud-specific features there.
3. Boosteroid (https://boosteroid.com/): It runs in a browser or apps on Windows, Android, macOS, iOS and Linux, which covers more device types than most rivals on this list. Pricing: Subscription-based; the page says any subscription gives unlimited gaming time. Plan prices are not in the readable text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing page returned no plan amounts in readable text, and the company and country were not stated on the pages we opened.
4. Shadow (https://shadow.tech/eu/): Shadow gives you a complete Windows machine, so any launcher or tool runs, at the cost of managing the install yourself. Pricing: Not stated in the extracted text of the opened pages. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Plan prices were not in the readable text of the opened pages, and the company name was not captured.
5. Amazon Luna (https://luna.amazon.com/): A rotating library with GameNight party games and no console needed, included with Prime on the Dutch page we opened. Pricing: Included with Prime, according to the Dutch Luna page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The only page we could read was the Dutch version, so regional availability and device lists are unconfirmed.
6. Blacknut (https://www.blacknut.com/en-us): Over 1,000 games, no playtime limit and clients for PC, Mac, phones, tablets and Smart TV make it a straightforward catalog subscription. Pricing: Subscription. The pricing page shows no plan prices in the extracted text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The English pricing page showed no plan amounts in readable text, and company and country details were not captured.
7. PlayStation Plus cloud streaming (https://www.playstation.com/en-us/ps-plus/): It adds cloud streaming to a membership that already covers online multiplayer and a catalog of PS4 and PS5 games. Pricing: Essential, Extra and Premium membership plans; plan prices are not in the extracted text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Plan prices were not in the readable text, and the page did not capture which devices can stream.
8. Loudplay (https://www.loudplay.io/): You buy hours on a cloud gaming PC and play titles you own, with prices published and no auto-renewal on desktop packs. Pricing: 3 hours for $3.99, 10 hours for $8.99, 20 hours for $15.99; Android plans are priced per region. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Hours expire after 30 days, clients cover Windows, macOS and Android only, and heavy players could spend more than on a flat subscription.
9. Antstream (https://www.antstream.com/): More than 1,300 officially licensed retro titles from publishers such as Atari, Bandai Namco and Disney, on PC, console, mobile and TV. Pricing: Subscription plans with annual and lifetime options; amounts are not in the extracted text of the pricing page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Amounts were not readable on the pricing page.
10. Parsec (https://parsec.app/): Parsec streams your own machine rather than a vendor library, with Pro and Teams plans and a trial. Pricing: Pro shown at $9.99 and $8.33, Teams at $35 and $30 (monthly versus annual billing), with a trial. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It needs a host computer, so it does not provide a game catalog or hardware.

## Best Community Chat Platforms for Gaming Communities in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-community-chat-platforms-for-gaming-communities
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A community chat platform for gaming is software where players, clans or a studio's fans talk in text channels, voice rooms or threaded forums. Some are hosted services with an account and server, some are self-hosted programs you run yourself, and some are open protocols that other apps build on top of.

1. Discord (https://discord.com/): Voice, text, video and streaming on PC, phone, console and browser, which is where most players already have an account. Pricing: The homepage shows no prices and links to a Nitro page (discord.com/nitro). Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage shows no prices and links to a Nitro page instead, so what a paying member or a server owner gets has to be checked elsewhere.
2. TeamSpeak (https://teamspeak.com/en/): Voice-first and server-based, with TeamSpeak 6 adding one-to-one voice and video calls and licensing moved to myTeamSpeak. Pricing: Server hosting licences are described on the licensing page; TeamSpeak 6 server licences are being moved to myTeamSpeak. Prices were not in the text read. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Licence prices were not in the text we read, so the cost of hosting a larger server is unclear.
3. Mumble (https://www.mumble.info): Free, open source and voice-only, with official client and server downloads for Windows and macOS. Pricing: Free and open source, per the site description. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The site notes that Linux distributions may ship their own packages with their own maintainers, so versions can differ.
4. Stoat (https://stoat.chat): An open-source alternative with servers, channels, voice chat and role-based permissions, free now and forever according to the vendor. Pricing: Free and open source, now and forever, per the vendor site; no subscription is needed for the extras it lists. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The site states a 20MB file upload limit, which is tight for sharing clips or builds.
5. Steam (https://store.steampowered.com): Valve's game store links discussions, a Workshop, a Market and broadcasts to the game itself. Pricing: No prices are shown on the pages opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices were shown on the pages opened.
6. Element (https://element.io/en): A client and server suite on the Matrix standard, with free self-hosted frontend and backend and per-seat server pricing. Pricing: The self-hosted frontend and backend are free of charge; the Element Server Suite is priced per seat per month, and enterprise plans are on the pricing page. Free option: Free. Falls short: It is aimed at secure collaboration and enterprise use, so gaming extras such as soundboards, activities or low-latency game voice are not in the facts we read.
7. Matrix (https://matrix.org): The open protocol behind clients such as Element, maintained by a foundation and not a chat app by itself. Pricing: Open protocol; the site shows no commercial pricing. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The site shows no commercial pricing or product tiers, so there is nobody to call for support unless you choose a commercial host.
8. Telegram (https://telegram.org): Cloud messaging on mobile and desktop, with communities, an open API and free source code. Pricing: No pricing is shown on the page opened; the page says the API and source code are free for everyone. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No pricing appears on the page we opened, and the facts do not mention gaming-specific features such as voice channels or event scheduling.
9. Discourse (https://discourse.org/): Open source forum software that can be self-hosted or managed, with real-time chat added to threaded discussion. Pricing: The codebase is described as freely available on GitHub; the homepage links to /pricing for hosting plans, with no amounts shown. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Pricing is not shown on the homepage; it links to a pricing page for hosting plans.
10. Spacebar (https://spacebar.chat): A free and open source, self-hosted platform that reimplements Discord, with docs, a web app and a GitHub repository. Pricing: Free and open source, per the site. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The facts show no hosted option, so someone must run the server.
11. Reddit (https://redditinc.com/): Thousands of interest-based communities where people post, vote and comment, but no voice or chat rooms in the facts. Pricing: No pricing is shown on the pages opened (the reddit.com home page is rendered by JavaScript and returned almost no text). Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The main reddit.com page returned almost no text to us, so facts rely on the company site.

## Best Community Management Tools for Game Studios in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-community-management-tools-for-game-studios
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Community management tools for game studios are the forums, chat servers, social listening dashboards and automation layers a community team uses to hear players and answer them. The category spans real-time chat, long-form discussion boards, publishing schedulers and listening products that track what players say elsewhere.

1. Discord (https://discord.com/): Discord leads because players already use it for voice, text and streaming on PC, phone and console. Pricing: No prices on the homepage; it links to a Nitro page (discord.com/nitro). Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Chat history is hard to search for newcomers, and the home page shows no prices, only a link to Nitro.
2. Khoros (https://khoros.ai/): Khoros takes second as a vendor combining a community platform with social listening, publishing and care. Pricing: No prices published; the vendor asks visitors to request a demo. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices are published and buyers are asked to request a demo.
3. Discourse (https://discourse.org/): Discourse ranks third as an open-source forum that studios can self-host or buy as a managed service. Pricing: The codebase is described as freely available on GitHub; the homepage links to /pricing for hosting plans, with no amounts shown. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Hosting plans link to a pricing page that shows no amounts on the home page, and self-hosting needs an engineer to keep it updated.
4. Vanilla (https://www.higherlogic.com/vanilla/): Vanilla sits fourth for studios that want a community tied to self-service support, with moderation tools. Pricing: No prices shown on the Vanilla page; it offers a Book a Demo button and a Packages link. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing is quote-only, with a Book a Demo button and a Packages link but no amounts.

## Best DDoS Protection for Game Servers in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-ddos-protection-for-game-servers
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

DDoS protection for game servers is a service or appliance that absorbs and filters flood attacks aimed at game hosts, whose traffic is mostly UDP and custom protocols rather than web requests. It works by routing traffic through scrubbing capacity or by filtering at the network edge, and the key trade-off is how much latency and routing change it adds for players.

1. OVHcloud (https://ovhcloud.com/): First because the homepage features a DDoS Protection Game offer for video games and e-sports, with protection included across its products. Pricing: Dedicated servers (Eco) from €13.99 excluding VAT per month, according to the homepage; the DDoS Protection Game offer is featured without a separate price on that page. Pricing: Homepage: 'Get Protected for Free' and 'Start protecting your network at no cost'. Plan names and prices are on a Pricing page that was not opened. Free option: Free. Falls short: Plan names and prices sit on a pricing page we did not open, and the named customers are Minecraft networks, so evidence for other game types or large studios is absent.
3. Gcore (https://gcore.com/): Third because the homepage cites 200Tbps of filtering capacity and a free start, plus a game studio among its case studies. Pricing: Homepage: 'Start for FREE' and 'Keep your citizen-facing sites and APIs protected at no cost until 31 December 2026.' A Pricing link is shown but no prices appear on the opened page. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The free offer in the homepage text is aimed at citizen-facing sites, not game servers, and no prices appear on the opened page.
4. Cloudflare (https://cloudflare.com/): Fourth because its network protects web layers well, but the page we opened did not describe raw UDP game server protection. Pricing: Homepage: 'Pay for What You Use', with CPU-time based billing, not wall-clock time. A 'See what it costs' link points to a plans page that was not opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Plan prices are not shown on the opened homepage, and a plans page was not opened.
5. Link11 (https://link11.com/): Fifth for its European base, always-on network mitigation with no surcharge and enterprise customers, though no game wording was found. Pricing: Homepage: 'Always-on, no surcharge' for network mitigation. A Pricing link is present but no figures or free-plan details are shown. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing link shows no figures, and the homepage names no game customers or UDP game traffic handling.
6. Akamai (https://akamai.com/): Sixth because Prolexic and a free-trial route suit large operators, while the opened page shows no game focus or price. Pricing: Homepage: 'Try Akamai Cloud with US$100 in credits' (footnoted); free trials are linked under Security and Delivery pricing. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No game wording, UDP detail or prices appear on the opened homepage, and the credits apply to Akamai Cloud rather than to DDoS protection.

Falls short: Services are described as subscription-based with no prices or free-plan details, and no game wording appears on the opened page.

Dedicated game server orchestration is the studio-side software that launches game server builds on demand, places them near players, scales fleets up and down, and reports their health. It sits between a matchmaker and the machines, and differs from renting a single server for a community.

1. Edgegap (https://edgegap.com/): Widest stated location reach, per-minute billing without a monthly fee, and matchmaking and lobbies bundled with orchestration. Pricing: Pay per minute on edge cloud with no upfront costs or fixed monthly fees; specific prices are not listed and a calculator is linked. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage gives no rates, only a pricing calculator link, and does not mention a free tier or trial.

Pricing: On demand $0.07 per vCPU per hour, reserved from $0.035, billed per second, bandwidth included. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It is matchmaker-agnostic, which means you bring your own matchmaking.

Falls short: No price amounts appear, only a demo request, so cost comparison needs sales contact.

## Best Esports Broadcast Production Software in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-esports-broadcast-production-software
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Esports broadcast production software is the layer between game feeds, observer clients, cameras, casters and the audience. It switches sources, plays replays, draws scoreboards and lower thirds, mixes audio and sends the finished program to a stream, a venue screen or both. Some products are full switchers; others only handle graphics or video transport.

1. vMix (https://www.vmix.com/): vMix packs switching, instant replay, NDI and SRT inputs and a title designer into one Windows program, with a published monthly price and a long trial. ## Best Game Anti-Cheat Software in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-anti-cheat-software
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Game anti-cheat software is a licensed security layer that detects cheats, tampering and exploit tools in an online game, then blocks or bans the offender. Approaches differ: some run protection on the player's machine, some analyze behavior on the server, and some harden the game binary itself. Studios usually integrate a client module, a server component and a ban and appeal workflow.

1. Easy Anti-Cheat (https://www.easy.ac/): First because a free service tier, cross-platform scope and a player appeals route make it the easiest licensing decision for a studio. Pricing: Free service tier plus paid Core, Fortified and Premier tiers. Paid tiers are arranged through a licensing contact form; no prices are shown. Free option: Free. Falls short: Paid tier prices are not shown and are arranged through a licensing contact form.
2. BattlEye (https://www.battleye.com): Second since it is an independent PC-focused service with documentation and support listed, though pricing needs a contact request. Pricing: Not published on the opened pages; the site has a contact page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing is not published on the opened pages; the site offers a contact page.
3. Anybrain (https://anybrain.gg): Third because it names PC, console and mobile coverage with an AI-based approach, but little detail was readable on its homepage. Pricing: No pricing shown on the opened page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage is JavaScript-rendered and little text could be read, and no pricing is shown.
4. Denuvo Anti-Cheat (https://irdeto.com/video-games): Fourth because it pairs cheat prevention with leak and piracy protection, useful to premium publishers, though pages stay general. 12. Digital.ai Application Protection (https://digital.ai/): Last because the opened pages describe application hardening inside a DevOps platform and say nothing about games or cheating. Pricing: Not shown on the opened pages; digital.ai/pricing returned 404. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The opened pages describe app hardening, not game anti-cheat, and no pricing is shown; the pricing URL returned a 404.

## Best Game Backend Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-backend-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A game backend platform is a hosted or self-run server layer that handles what a live game needs outside the client: player identity, saved progress, virtual currency and inventory, leaderboards, matchmaking hooks and scheduled content. Studios call it through SDKs and APIs instead of writing and operating a custom backend.

1. PlayFab (https://playfab.com/): Broadest published feature list, console and storefront integrations, and a free start make it the safest default for a studio that wants one vendor for most backend work. Pricing: Free to start, then pay-as-you-go, with no dollar figures on the product page. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The page shows no dollar figures, so budgeting needs a separate calculation.
2. AccelByte (https://accelbyte.io/): The only entry with a worked cost example on its homepage, plus entitlements, leaderboards and multiplayer servers in modular pieces. Pricing: First 30 CCU free during development, no monthly platform fee on Public Cloud after the trial, and usage-based billing that scales with peak concurrency. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Billing follows peak concurrent players, so the bill moves with success and spiky launches.
3. Metaplay (https://metaplay.io/): Delivers the backend as readable source with built-in segments, offers and remote configs, which suits teams that want control without writing everything. Pricing: Free tier to build and run locally, Pro tier for cloud deployment with no price shown, Enterprise tier for self-hosting at scale. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The Pro tier shows no price, and the page does not list supported client engines, only a Unity testimonial.
4. Nakama (https://heroiclabs.com/): The most established open source option, with server scripting in three languages and a long customer list. Pricing: Open source download is available; the homepage names no license or price and links to a pricing page for hosted plans. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The homepage names no license, which matters before commercial use.
5. Pragma (https://pragma.gg/): A studio-scale backend with authentication, orders, telemetry and admin dashboards, held back by a homepage that shows no prices or SDK list. Pricing: The homepage links to a pricing page but states no prices and no free tier. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage gives no price amounts, no free tier, and no named engines or SDKs, so a small team cannot judge fit without a call.
6. Beamable (https://beamable.com/): Replaces custom backend work with hosted services and native SDKs, with a trial measured in API calls and a credit program. Pricing: Start for Free leads to a pricing page with no plan prices; trial usage is up to 1,000,000 free API calls. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No plan prices appear on the homepage, and the trial figure is printed as '1000,000', which suggests the page needs a second look before you rely on it.
7. Unity Live Services (Unity Gaming Services) (https://unity.com/solutions/gaming-services): A deep list of live features such as Cloud Code, Cloud Save and A/B testing for Unity projects, but a page with no prices or platform names. Pricing: Get started for free and a View Pricing link, with no figures or tier details on the page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The page does not use the name Unity Gaming Services and shows no prices.
8. LootLocker (https://lootlocker.com/): A free-to-start platform built around player relationships, content and live systems, and aimed at publishers of many small titles. Pricing: Free to start; the pricing page is linked but shows no figures or free-tier details. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The homepage names no engines, platforms or SDK languages, and the pricing page, as linked, lists no figures, so cost beyond the free start is unclear.
9. Steamworks (https://partner.steamgames.com/): Inventory, microtransactions and lobbies for games sold on Steam, but of no use off the storefront. Pricing: Joining needs paperwork and a small per-app fee; no revenue-share terms are given on the page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It works only with Steam, so console and mobile players are out of reach.
10. Firebase (https://firebase.google.com/): A general application platform with Remote Config and Crashlytics, usable for games but missing game-specific economy and leaderboard modules. Pricing: $300 in credit when you create a Billing Account; no free-plan or pay-as-you-go figures on the homepage. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The homepage lists no game modules such as inventory, currency or leaderboards, so you write those rules yourself.
11. Supabase (https://supabase.com/): Open source and self-hostable with Postgres, auth and realtime, but it offers no game-specific modules. Pricing: A Free plan exists, free projects pause after 7 days of low activity, and the homepage shows no other prices. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Free-plan projects pause after 7 days of low activity, which hurts a quiet prototype.

## Best Game Capture and Recording Software in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-capture-and-recording-software
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Game capture and recording software saves gameplay video from a PC while you play, either as continuous recordings or as short clips of recent moments. Most tools add editing, a clip library or sharing links, and many use the graphics card to keep frame-rate loss low.

1. Outplayed (https://outplayed.tv/): Outplayed records your best plays by itself, adds an editor and performance tracking, and offers a Free tier with a Premium upgrade. Pricing: Free and Premium tiers. Premium removes ads and unlocks premium features; prices were not on the opened page. Free option: Free. Falls short: The Free tier carries ads, and the page we opened did not publish Premium prices.
2. Medal (https://medal.tv/): Medal is a free PC app for recording, editing and sharing game clips, with a games library behind it. Pricing: Free to download and use on PC, per the homepage meta description. Free option: Free. Falls short: The facts we gathered mention PC only and give no technical specifications, supported-game list or paid tiers, so the long-term cost is unclear.
3. NVIDIA App (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/nvidia-app/): The NVIDIA App bundles ShadowPlay and driver updates, so GeForce owners can record without installing a separate recorder at all. Pricing: The download page is region-specific and shows no price. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It requires an NVIDIA GPU on a Windows PC, and the page we read states no price or limits.
4. OBS Studio (https://obsproject.com/): OBS Studio records on Windows, macOS and Linux for free, with scenes built from game, window and webcam sources. Pricing: Free and open source software. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Nothing about clipping, highlights or sharing appears in the vendor facts, so it is a recorder, not a clip service.
5. Mirillis Action (https://mirillis.com/): Mirillis Action from Mirillis records games and the desktop at up to 120 FPS, with 4K webcam and HDR options, on Windows. Pricing: The homepage offers a free trial download and a purchase option; prices were not on the opened page. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The page we opened did not show a price, only a trial download and Buy Mirillis Action options.
6. Bandicam (https://www.bandicam.com/): Bandicam captures the screen, gameplay and webcam on Windows, with built-in editing, an audio recorder and AI tools. Pricing: Bandicam has a free version and a full version; the homepage links to a free vs full version comparison. Prices were not on the opened pages. Free option: Free. Falls short: Prices were not on the pages we opened, so the cost of the full version is unknown.
7. Allstar (https://allstar.gg/): Allstar describes free clip capture with zero FPS drop for Counter-Strike 2, League of Legends, Fortnite and Dota 2, with apps on iOS and Android. Pricing: The homepage calls clip capture free; subscriptions and product tiers exist but no prices appeared on the pages opened. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Game coverage on the homepage is four titles, which excludes most libraries.
8. AMD Software Adrenalin (https://www.amd.com/en/products/software/adrenalin.html): AMD Software Adrenalin bundles driver updates, game stats and in-game capture for AMD products on a Windows PC. Pricing: No price is shown; the vendor page presents it as software for AMD products. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It works only with AMD products on a Windows PC.
9. ShareX (https://getsharex.com/): ShareX is a free, open source Windows tool for screenshots, screen recording and GIFs, with automation after capture. Pricing: Completely free, with no advertisements; the footer says 'Free forever. Open source. No account required.' A Donate page is linked. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Windows is the only platform the page names, and gaming is not its main purpose, so it offers no automatic highlight capture.
10. Fraps (https://fraps.com/): Fraps shows frame rate, takes screenshots and records video in DirectX and OpenGL games on Windows, with a last release in 2013. Pricing: A free download is offered; the paid full version requires registration and no price appears on the download page. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The download page gives the latest release as Fraps 3.5.99, dated February 26, 2013, so newer games and Windows builds may not be supported.

## Best Game CI/CD and Build Tools in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-ci-cd-and-build-tools
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Game CI/CD and build tools automate compiling, testing, signing and delivering a game build whenever code or assets change. They include hosted pipeline services, self-hosted build servers and distributed compilers, and they matter more for games than for web apps because builds are large, slow and aimed at several platforms.

1. GameCI (https://game.ci/): MIT-licensed Unity build tooling that runs on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and CircleCI, at no licence cost. Pricing: GameCI is free with no licence fees, per its page; sponsorship through OpenCollective is optional. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Unity is the only engine listed, so Unreal and Godot teams get nothing from it.
2. Jenkins (https://www.jenkins.io/): A self-hosted build server that runs anywhere and can drive any engine through plugins and scripts. Pricing: The vendor page states no price; Jenkins is described as open source and runs on hardware you provide. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The opened page names no licence and no game-specific features.
3. FASTBuild (https://www.fastbuild.org/): A compile accelerator that spreads C++ work across machines and caches results, rather than a full CI service. Pricing: The vendor page does not state a price; FASTBuild is described as open source. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It is a compiler driver, not a CI platform: no scheduling, no dashboards, no artifact handling on the opened page.
4. TeamCity (https://www.jetbrains.com/teamcity/): A commercial CI server from JetBrains that scales by adding build agents, though the opened page is sparse. Pricing: JetBrains does not show prices in the text we opened; the buy page is titled Pricing and Licensing, More Build Agents and links a Try free download. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Our fetch returned minimal text, so we could not confirm features, supported platforms or price figures.
5. Azure DevOps (https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/devops/): Pipelines run in parallel on three operating systems and deploy to any cloud or on-premises target. Pricing: The product page states no plan prices and mentions flexible licensing for bundles and pay as you go. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No plan prices or free tier limits appear on the opened page, and nothing there is specific to games or consoles.
6. GitHub (https://github.com/): The Actions feature supplies the runner that GameCI and many custom pipelines build on. Pricing: The homepage offers an Enterprise free trial and links to plans and pricing, but no prices appear on the opened page. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Plan prices are not shown on the opened homepage, and it says nothing about macOS or Windows runner costs, build minutes or large Unity cache needs.
7. Bitrise (https://bitrise.io/): Managed mobile build service on Apple silicon and Linux machines, with a free tier. Pricing: Bitrise says a free tier with managed cloud build infrastructure is available, and CodePush is free up to 100K monthly active users; other figures sit on a pricing page we did not open. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The opened page does not name Unity or Unreal, and a Windows build for PC is not mentioned.
8. Codemagic (https://codemagic.io/): Cloud builds for Flutter, native apps and Unity, configured through a YAML file. Pricing: Codemagic gives no figures on its home page: it offers usage-based or unlimited usage and points to a separate pricing page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices are on the home page, and we did not open the pricing page.
9. Appcircle (https://appcircle.io/): Mobile build, test and publish tooling with a self-hosted option, though game engines are not named. Pricing: The home page shows a Start for Free button and lists no prices. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The page does not name Unity or Unreal, and no prices are listed beyond a free start button.
10. Xcode Cloud (https://developer.apple.com/xcode-cloud/): Published compute-hour pricing and TestFlight integration, but only for Apple platforms and Apple Developer members. Pricing: Apple Developer Program membership includes 25 compute hours a month; paid tiers run from US$49.99 a month for 100 hours to US$3,999.99 for 10,000 hours. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Membership in the Apple Developer Program is required, and the page notes that EU-based organizations are subject to additional Xcode Cloud terms under Regulation (EU) 2023/2854.

## Best Game Engines for Mobile Games in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-engines-for-mobile-games
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A mobile game engine is software that builds games for phones and tablets: it handles touch input, rendering, packaging for iOS and Android, and often connects to ad networks, in-app purchases and analytics. Some engines are full editors, others are code libraries or no-code builders. This ranking uses what each vendor publishes about targets and monetization.

1. Unity (https://unity.com/): The only entry whose own page lists purchase, monetization and user acquisition services next to the engine. Pricing: The homepage says to start free or find a plan, and shows no price figures or tier names. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices or paid-tier names are on the homepage, so budgeting for monetization services needs the plans page.
2. Solar2D (https://solar2d.com/): Phone targets, TV boxes and a plugin system, all without fees, make it a lean pick for small mobile teams. Pricing: Free under the MIT license; no hidden fees, charges or royalties, according to the homepage. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The facts do not list specific ad or purchase plugins, so check the plugin directory before assuming your network is supported.
3. Defold (https://defold.com/): Mobile and portal targets plus Live Update and native extensions make it a strong free option for phone teams. Pricing: Free forever under a source-available license, with no up-front cost, licensing cost, royalties or runtime fee. Free option: Free. Falls short: The license is source available, not open source.
4. Godot (https://godotengine.org/): Free and open, with mobile export and a separate 2D renderer, but no stated store-SDK or monetization features. Pricing: No cost. Described as free and open source; no further pricing statement or license name is on the homepage. Free option: Open source. Falls short: No ad, purchase or analytics integrations are named in the facts, and build size is not stated.
5. GDevelop (https://gdevelop.io/): Clicks instead of code and one-click Android and iOS publishing, with iOS gated behind the upper plan. Pricing: Open-source engine with paid Silver and Gold plans; iOS export is on the higher plan and no prices appear in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: iOS publishing needs the higher paid plan, and amounts are not shown in the page text.
6. Stencyl (https://stencyl.com/): Names in-app purchases, ads and store sales on its homepage, but publishes no price and mentions an older ad network. Pricing: A Pricing section exists, but the homepage prints no plans or figures. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices or plan names are published, and iAds appears in its ad network list, suggesting text that may be dated.
7. Cocos Creator (https://cocos.com/): Heavy partner list and a full toolchain, but no stated platforms, license or price to confirm a phone fit. Pricing: The homepage lists no price or license; it shows a download button and a store link. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Without itemized platforms, price or license, a buyer cannot verify mobile suitability or cost from the page.
8. Phaser (https://github.com/phaserjs/phaser): Fits phone browsers and social portals, but native app store builds depend on separate wrapper tools. Pricing: Free under MIT, per the official repository page. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Store builds rely on third-party wrappers, and the page does not name ad or purchase plugins.
9. LOVE (https://love2d.org/): A Lua framework with touch input and Android and iOS packages, though the iOS route is source, not a ready build. Pricing: Free, with unlimited commercial use under the zlib/libpng license. Free option: Open source. Falls short: iOS needs you to build from source and libraries.
10. Bevy (https://bevy.org/): Lists iOS and Android with permissive licensing, but offers no editor or store-service tools. Pricing: No license fees or sales cuts; MIT or Apache 2.0, with optional donor tiers from $25 to $6,000 monthly. Free option: Open source. Falls short: No editor is in the feature list, and mobile store workflow details are missing from the facts.
11. Buildbox (https://buildbox.com/): A no-code game maker with a hint of Android work, but no stated price, platform or feature detail. Pricing: Not stated; a Get Buildbox link leads to a download page without a price or trial. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Nothing about platforms, store SDKs, monetization or cost is stated on the page.
12. GB Studio (https://gbstudio.dev/): Makes retro Game Boy games and exports web builds with mobile controls, not native store apps. Pricing: No price is stated; the page links to a download on Itch.io and to Patreon. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It does not list native iOS or Android builds, ads or in-app purchases, so it is no fit for store monetization.

## Best Game Launchers and Library Managers in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-launchers-and-library-managers
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A game launcher is the desktop app a store or publisher uses to download, update and start its games. A library manager sits above the stores and merges several launchers' collections into one searchable list, often with playtime, tags and controller-friendly screens. Some tools also handle emulators or a single game such as Minecraft.

1. Playnite (https://playnite.link/): Playnite is free and open source, imports from Steam, Epic, Origin, GOG, Battle.net and Ubisoft Connect, and adds themes and extensions. Pricing: Completely free. Playnite is open source. Free option: Free. Falls short: The pages we read state no platform list, and the integrations depend on plugins keeping pace with store changes.
2. GOG Galaxy (https://www.gog.com/galaxy): GOG Galaxy combines multiple game libraries into one and connects friends across platforms, consoles included. Pricing: Pricing for the GOG Galaxy client is not stated on the opened page. The GOG store sells DRM-free games with a 30-day money-back guarantee. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The price of the client itself is not stated on the opened page.
3. Heroic Games Launcher (https://heroicgameslauncher.com): Heroic is a free GPLv3 launcher for Epic, GOG and Amazon Prime Games on Linux, Windows, macOS and the Steam Deck. Pricing: Free. The homepage says there is no paid tier, and the FAQ says Heroic is completely free to use. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It covers three stores, not every one, and Steam is not among its named services.
4. Lutris (https://lutris.net): Lutris installs and launches games on Linux from Steam, Epic, GOG and Humble Bundle libraries, with emulators and compatibility layers. Pricing: Free and open source. The homepage says Lutris is built only using open source technology, and it has a Donate link. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It is Linux only, so Windows and Mac players cannot use it.
5. Steam (https://store.steampowered.com): Steam is Valve's digital store and community platform, with workshop, market, broadcasts and Remote Play, but only for its own catalog. Pricing: No prices are shown on the pages opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pages we read show no prices for the client, and no feature for importing other stores.
6. LaunchBox (https://www.launchbox-app.com/): LaunchBox is a portable box-art games database and launcher for DOSBox, emulators and arcade cabinets, free with a paid Premium license. Pricing: LaunchBox for Windows is available for free download. The Premium license can be renewed for $15 for another year of updates, or upgraded for $45 to a never-expiring forever-updates license. Free option: Free. Falls short: The page we read does not describe Steam, Epic or GOG importers in detail, so modern store libraries are not its focus.
7. Battle.net (https://download.battle.net/en-us/desktop): Battle.net launches Blizzard games from one app, with friends, voice chat, two-factor authentication and a shop. Pricing: Download is free. The download page says some titles can be played for free and that free trials are available for many titles; other games and goodies are sold in the shop. Free option: Free. Falls short: It manages Blizzard-family games only and cannot merge other stores.
8. Ubisoft Connect (https://www.ubisoft.com/en-us/ubisoft-connect): Ubisoft Connect is a free multi-platform service for Ubisoft games with chat, friends, rewards and cross-progression. Pricing: Free service that only requires a Ubisoft account. Free option: Free. Falls short: It shows Ubisoft's own games and offers no multi-store library.
9. EA app (https://www.ea.com/ea-app): The EA app downloads and plays EA games on PC and links EA Play offers, with games sold separately. Pricing: Pricing is not stated on the opened page. The page links an EA Play offer and EA app deals; individual games are sold separately. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing is not stated on the opened page, and games are sold separately.
10. Prism Launcher (https://prismlauncher.org/): Prism Launcher manages multiple Minecraft instances, accounts and mods, with Modrinth and CurseForge integration, and is free and open source. Pricing: Free; the project accepts donations and publishes under open-source licenses. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It handles Minecraft only, so it cannot hold a general game library.

A game LiveOps platform is the toolset a team uses after launch to schedule events, adjust remote configuration, personalize offers for player segments, run experiments and measure results, usually without a client update. It may be a full backend suite or a standalone layer on top of one.

1. Metaplay (https://metaplay.io/): Ships events, over-the-air configs, A/B tests, segments and offers with a dashboard, on top of a server-authoritative backend. Pricing: Free tier for local builds, Pro tier for cloud deployment with no price shown, Enterprise for self-hosting. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Adopting it means taking the backend too, so it is not a bolt-on for an existing server.

Pricing: Heroic Cloud plans, covering Nakama and Satori, start from $600 per month, with bespoke pricing through sales. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No separate Satori price is shown, only the Heroic Cloud starting figure.

Falls short: The page does not break down event scheduling, segmentation or experiments, so depth must be verified in documentation.

Pricing: Start for Free leads to a pricing page without plan prices; trial usage is up to 1,000,000 free API calls. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No plan prices are visible, and API-call based trials can run out fast during load tests.
5. AccelByte (https://accelbyte.io/): A modular multiplatform backend where achievements, entitlements and sessions support live operations, though event tooling is not itemized. Pricing: First 30 CCU free in development, no monthly platform fee on Public Cloud after the trial, usage-based on peak concurrency. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Event calendars, remote config and experiments are not named on the homepage, so LiveOps depth is unconfirmed.

Pricing: Get started for free and a View Pricing link; the page shows no figures or tier details. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices or tier details are shown, and engines other than Unity are not mentioned.
7. Balancy (https://en.docs.balancy.dev/): A plugin for offers, inventory, purchases, events, battle passes and A/B tests, documented in detail but with no readable pricing. Pricing: Not found on the pages we opened; the homepage rendered through JavaScript and the www host showed a certificate error. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The marketing homepage rendered with no readable text for our fetcher, and we found no price, company or platform list.

Pricing: The homepage links a pricing page but states no price amounts and no free tier. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices, no free tier and no listed engines or SDKs.

Pricing: $300 in credit when you create a Billing Account; no free-plan figures shown on the homepage. Free option: Free trial. Pricing: Developer tier free with 2M events per month; a $150 tier includes 5M events, then $0.05 per 1K events. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The pages we read describe general product development, not game events, currency or offers, so those need custom work.

## Best Game Localization Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-localization-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Game localization platforms manage the text, and sometimes audio, that must be translated for each market. They store strings from the game, send them to translators or machine translation, check quality and return finished files to the build. Service vendors add linguists, testing and voice work on top of the software.

1. Gridly (https://www.gridly.com/): Describes itself as tailor-made for game development, with a grid-style content system and published starting prices. Pricing: Gridly lists CMS from EUR 99 a month with 3 seats and extra seats at EUR 29; TMS and CAT are priced separately, and a 14-day trial covers all modules. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: TMS and CAT modules are priced separately, and the price shown on the opened page was cut off, so total cost for a full stack needs a quote.
2. Crowdin (https://crowdin.com/): Free plan, Git sync, built-in QA checks and in-context preview, listing games among the content types it supports. Pricing: Crowdin says a free plan is available, with paid Team and Enterprise plans and a Contact Sales option; organization plans are billed annually only. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The page does not name any game engine plugin, and organization plans are billed annually only.
3. Lokalise (https://lokalise.com/): Publishes monthly prices from USD 149, with AI scoring, workflows and a translation API. Pricing: Lokalise lists Explorer at USD 149, Growth at USD 379 and Advanced at USD 1,049 per month billed monthly, with Enterprise by demo and a free 14-day trial without a credit card. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Nothing on the opened pages mentions games, string tables for dialogue or engine plugins.
4. Phrase (https://phrase.com/): TMS, software localization and quality evaluation under one vendor, with a 14-day trial. Pricing: Phrase lists Business, Developer and designer, and Freelancer and LSP plans with a 14-day trial; the Premium Success Plan and higher tiers are custom, and prices can show in EUR, USD, GBP and CZK. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No game focus is stated on the opened pages, and plan prices are not shown there.
5. Transifex (https://www.transifex.com/): Lists Game Localization as a use case, with a CLI, SDKs and a usage-based plan. Pricing: Transifex says one plan includes every capability and customers pay for AI-translated words at a rate that improves with volume; human review and post-editing do not count toward usage. Falls short: No game-specific features are listed and no prices appear on the opened plans page.

Falls short: Rates are approximate, and the opened pages describe no in-engine plugin or string table tool.

Falls short: No prices are published and no tool or plugin is described on the opened pages.

## Best Game Market Intelligence Tools in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-market-intelligence-tools
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Game market intelligence tools collect and model public store data, panel data and publisher feeds to estimate how other games perform. They report downloads, revenue, owners, wishlists, live events and audience mix by title, genre or region. Studios use them to judge a pitch, pick a genre, benchmark a launch and set realistic sales targets.

1. Sensor Tower (https://sensortower.com/): First because it covers the widest range of data, from app performance to ad spend, includes a gaming product and offers a free start. Pricing: Paid prices are not listed; the home page has a Sign Up for Free button and a free Chrome extension, Web Insights, plus Request Demo and Contact Sales options. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Paid prices are not listed, and the breadth means a studio that needs only Steam data pays for a platform much larger than its question.
2. GameDiscoverCo (https://gamediscover.co/): Second because wishlist data, console coverage and forecasts from comparable games speak directly to a PC or console launch plan. Pricing: No prices on the home page; features are sold under GameDiscoverCo Pro, and the page offers Book a demo and Ask about access. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices are shown, and MCP access depends on a Pro plan with access enabled, so the cheapest route in is unclear.

Pricing: The pricing page lets you build your own feature set from dashboards, tools and data access; prices are not in the fetched text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The home page is rendered by JavaScript, so we took facts from its meta description; prices are not visible and the company is not named in the text we read.
4. VGInsights (https://app.sensortower.com/vgi/): Fourth because 50+ datapoints for over 150,000 games give depth for comparables, while the product now lives inside Sensor Tower. Pricing: Pricing is not shown in the fetched text; the product has a pricing page hosted on app.sensortower.com. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The vendor page is rendered by JavaScript and we could read only the meta description; prices and platform coverage are not visible.

Falls short: The home page does not show prices, free access or how the estimates are produced, and the pricing page was not opened.
6. Game Refinery (https://www.gamerefinery.com/): Sixth because live events, mechanics and player motivation data suit live-ops planning, though it covers mobile and shows no paid prices. Falls short: It is mobile-centered, no paid prices are shown, and what the free access includes is not described.

Falls short: Plan limits and tiers are not described on the home page, so it is unclear what the free start includes.

Pricing: Custom pricing; the investor pricing page says the base package is an enterprise-level service, with flexible plans for brands and for MSP and sales teams. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Its pages are written for investors, brands and sales teams, not game developers, and the base package is described as enterprise-level with custom pricing.

Pricing: Not stated on the opened page; the page offers a NikoIQ demo and contact options. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Coverage is limited to Asia and MENA, no prices are shown, and the product is research and consulting rather than a self-serve dataset.
