Pricing: No prices appear on the opened pages; the About page calls it a side project of its author. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The About page says the site is still in beta and often wrong, owners do not equal sales, and the copyright range is 2015-2021, so freshness is a concern.

## Best Game Payment and Web Shop Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-payment-and-web-shop-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A game payment and web shop platform lets a studio sell items, currency or games to players outside the app stores. It hosts the web store and checkout, accepts local payment methods, and in many cases acts as merchant of record, taking over sales tax, VAT, fraud handling and chargebacks so the studio does not register in each market itself.

1. Xsolla (https://www.xsolla.com/): Ranks first because it is the only vendor here that pairs a games-specific web shop with payments, publishing and live-ops tooling under one roof. Pricing: Not stated on the opened pages; the pricing URL leads to a contact form, and the homepage says tools launch with no upfront costs. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No rate card is shown; the pricing link ends at a contact form, so the up to 95% claim cannot be checked against fees before a sales call.
2. Appcharge (https://www.appcharge.com/): Second because it is built for one job, selling mobile in-game items through branded stores, and states merchant of record, 500+ methods and 100+ currencies. Pricing: Not stated on the opened pages; the /pricing URL returns 404 and the site uses contact forms. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Mobile only, so PC and console studios will not find a fit.
3. Coda Payments (https://www.coda.co/): Third because it is the one games-focused vendor that prints per-transaction rates and still offers a webstore and merchant of record. Pricing: Standard rates start from 1% per transaction, with other standard rates of 5% and a flat 15% per transaction; custom pricing for companies expecting at least $100K USD of volume per month. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing page does not say which product each of the three rates applies to in the text we read, so you still need to ask what 1% versus 15% buys.
4. Stash (https://www.stash.gg/): Fourth because it bundles a webshop, launcher and loyalty program with merchant of record, but gives less on payment coverage and price. Pricing: Not published; the site offers a Contact Sales link. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The coverage figure shown, 64 countries and 21 currencies, is a single customer's footprint rather than a platform total, and no payment-method count appears.
5. Aghanim (https://aghanim.com/): Fifth because the performance-based, no-upfront-cost model suits a small mobile studio, but the opened pages give no fees or payment coverage. Pricing: Not stated on the opened pages; the About page describes a performance-based model with no upfront costs. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Neither the homepage nor the About page states fee percentages, payment-method counts or currency coverage, so reach cannot be compared with Xsolla or Appcharge.
6. Tebex (https://www.tebex.io/): Sixth because it has the largest self-reported merchant base and a store-protection product, but the pages show less detail on tax handling. Pricing: Not stated on the page; the site offers Talk to sales and Open Account buttons. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage does not say whether Tebex acts as merchant of record, and shows no fees.
7. FastSpring (https://fastspring.com/): Seventh because it is a full merchant of record with a flat-rate pitch and a video games use case, but it is not built around live-ops offers. Pricing: One flat rate with no hidden fees, per the pricing page headline; the rate itself is not in the opened text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It targets software and digital goods broadly, so there is no games-specific storefront, loyalty or live-ops layer in the pages we read.
8. Paddle (https://www.paddle.com/): Eighth because the merchant of record is solid for subscriptions and names Nexus Mods as a customer, yet it describes itself as made for SaaS and apps. Pricing: The pricing page says it shows Paddle's fees and offers a custom enterprise quote; the fee figures are not in the captured page text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The positioning is SaaS and apps first, with no in-game item shop, offers engine or launcher.
9. Paymentwall (https://www.paymentwall.com/): Ninth because local-method coverage is wide and plugins exist, but it is a payment provider rather than a game store. Pricing: Not stated on the opened pages; the site invites a consultation. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No game-specific storefront, offers or launcher is described, and merchant-of-record status is not stated on the pages we opened.
10. Boku (https://www.boku.com/): Tenth because carrier billing and wallet reach help in card-light markets, though it supplies payment rails rather than a shop. Pricing: Not stated on the page; it offers a Talk to an expert contact. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It is a payments network, not a web shop, and the homepage does not state merchant-of-record status or fees.
11. Nuvei (https://www.nuvei.com/): Eleventh because the infrastructure is deep, with over 720 payment options and gaming use cases, but it targets larger teams and publishes no price. Pricing: Not stated on the page; merchants are directed to contact sales. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It does not ship a games web shop or offers engine, and it directs merchants to contact sales for any price.
12. Adyen (https://www.adyen.com/): Twelfth because the fee structure is stated and coverage is wide, yet it is an enterprise processor and leaves store, tax and compliance to you. Pricing: Pay per transaction with no setup or monthly fees: a fixed processing fee plus a fee set by the payment method, per the pricing page. Free option: None. Falls short: It provides no games web shop, offers or merchant-of-record service in the pages we opened, so tax, fraud policy and store design stay with you.
13. Stripe (https://stripe.com/en-nl): Thirteenth because it is the most flexible set of payment building blocks, yet nothing on the opened pages is specific to games. Pricing: The Pricing and Fees page lists processing fees, pricing models and pay-as-you-go fees; the figures are not in the captured page text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: None of the opened pages mention games, a web shop for in-game items, offers, or merchant-of-record status, so everything beyond the payment itself is your build.

## Best Game QA and Test Automation Tools in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-game-qa-and-test-automation-tools
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Game QA and test automation tools verify that a game works on the platforms it ships on. Engine-aware frameworks inspect objects inside Unity or Unreal, UI automation tools tap screens, device clouds provide real phones to run builds on, and managed services supply human testers. Studios combine several because no single approach covers rendering, logic, devices and play feel.

1. AltTester (https://alttester.com/): First because it names both Unity and Unreal, covers mobile, PC, console, WebGL and AR/VR, and offers a free trial. Falls short: No prices or free-plan details are shown on the opened page, only a pricing link and a trial button.

Pricing: Not stated on the opened page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The opened page names no license and no developer company, and pricing is not stated.
3. modl.ai (https://modl.ai/): Third because AI agents test builds without SDKs or code changes, though iOS and console support are still in progress. Pricing: Not published on the opened homepage; visitors are asked to book a demo or click Get started (contact page). Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Android and desktop are supported today, iOS is in development and console workflows are still being expanded, according to the homepage.
4. Appium (https://appium.io/): Fourth because the open-source framework reaches iOS, Android, desktop and TV, but sees UI elements, not engine objects. Pricing: Not stated on the opened page. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Nothing on the opened page addresses game engines, so gameplay tests depend on screen positions or image tricks that break after UI changes.
5. Kobiton (https://kobiton.com/): Fifth because it provides real devices with scriptless options and cites an unnamed US gaming company among its audience. Pricing: Self-serve plans starting at $83 per month; a higher plan starting at $399 per month; quotes for larger needs through a contact page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The gaming company is unnamed, plan details are not shown on the opened page, and named customers are banks and telecoms.
6. BrowserStack (https://www.browserstack.com/): Sixth because its device and browser coverage is wide and trusted, but the page describes no game testing. Pricing: Plans start at $12.50 a month according to the pricing page title; monthly or annual plans for freelancers, teams and enterprises. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Plan prices are not stated on the homepage, and nothing there refers to games, engines or GPU-intensive workloads.
7. Sauce Labs (https://saucelabs.com/): Seventh because it offers real and virtual device clouds and AI authoring, but targets enterprise software releases. Pricing: Homepage button 'Try Sauce AI FOR FREE'; no other pricing details are stated. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Positioning is enterprise software, and nothing on the page mentions games.
8. LambdaTest (TestMu AI) (https://www.testmuai.com/): Eighth because it combines AI test tools with a device cloud, though it was renamed in January 2026 and shows no game focus. Pricing: 'Start free with Email', 'Start free with Google' and 'Get Started For Free' are shown; enterprise via 'Book a Demo' and 'Contact Sales'; no prices stated. Free option: Free. Falls short: Prices are not stated, only free sign-up and a contact route for enterprise.

Falls short: The opened homepage does not describe a playtesting product, and contracts are tailored to scope with no published prices.
10. Testlio (https://www.testlio.com/): Tenth because crowdsourced testers and a platform handle manual, regression and localization checks, without any playtesting mention. Pricing: Not published on the opened pricing page, which links to Contact sales. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The opened homepage does not mention playtesting, and plan prices are not stated.

## Best Hardware Monitoring and Overclocking Software in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-hardware-monitoring-and-overclocking-software
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Hardware monitoring and overclocking software reads the sensors inside a PC: temperatures, fan speeds, voltages, clock speeds and power. Some tools also tune processor behavior or run stress tests to prove a configuration is stable. Gamers use them to catch throttling, builders to validate cooling, and studios to keep test machines healthy.

1. HWiNFO (https://www.hwinfo.com): HWiNFO reports in-depth hardware data and live sensors, logs to file and shows an on-screen display, free for personal use. Pricing: Free for personal and non-commercial use. Commercial use of HWiNFO 64 or ARM64 requires the Pro license. The licenses page lists Pro initial prices from $29 and $199 and a renewal price from $14.50 (renewal price shown as 14.5). Free option: Free. Falls short: Free use stops at personal and non-commercial environments, so a company fleet needs the Pro license.
2. OCCT (https://www.ocbase.com): OCCT combines stability and stress testing, benchmarks and monitoring for Windows and Linux, free for personal use. Pricing: OCCT Personal is free for personal use and cannot be used in a commercial or business environment. Pro, Enterprise and Enterprise+ licenses are required for business use. The download page says a subscription is available via Patreon to support development. Free option: Free. Falls short: OCCT Personal is limited to non-commercial use, and the prices of the business editions are not in our facts.
3. HWMonitor (https://www.cpuid.com/softwares/hwmonitor.html): HWMonitor reads voltages, temperatures, powers, currents, fan speeds, utilizations and clocks on Windows, with a PRO edition available. Pricing: The standard HWMonitor is offered free. An extended HWMonitor PRO version is also offered; its price is not shown on the opened page. Free option: Free. Falls short: The price of HWMonitor PRO is not shown on the opened page, and the free version offers no stress testing or logging details in our facts.
4. LibreHardwareMonitor (https://github.com/LibreHardwareMonitor/LibreHardwareMonitor): LibreHardwareMonitor is free open source software for temperatures, fan speeds, voltages, loads and clocks, published on GitHub. Pricing: Free software. The repository links a LICENSE file and a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES file. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The repository page gives no platform list and no help-desk path beyond the project itself.
5. CPU-Z (https://www.cpuid.com/softwares/cpu-z.html): CPU-Z shows processor, mainboard, chipset and memory details, measures core frequency live, and runs on Windows and Android. Pricing: Freeware. Free option: Free. Falls short: It is an inspector rather than a monitor of temperatures and fans, so you need a second tool for sensors.
6. AIDA64 (https://www.aida64.com): AIDA64 mixes hardware detection, real-time sensor monitoring, stress tests, benchmarks and overclocking support in paid editions. Pricing: Pricing is not shown on the opened pages. AIDA64 is licensed with a product key; the licensing page describes support and maintenance periods, renewals, and trial versions. Editions are Extreme, Engineer, Business and Network Audit. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Prices are not shown on the opened pages, only license terms with product keys and renewable maintenance.
7. Ryzen Master (https://www.amd.com/en/products/software/ryzen-master.html): Ryzen Master gives control over AMD Ryzen processors with performance profiles, monitoring and a Curve Optimizer feature. Pricing: Pricing is not stated on the opened product page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It works only with AMD Ryzen processors, and the opened page states no price or platform details.
8. Prime95 (https://www.mersenne.org/download/): Prime95 is free GIMPS software for Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and macOS that uses spare processing power to search for primes. Pricing: Free. The GIMPS download page offers the software free of charge. Free option: Free. Falls short: The pages we read say nothing about monitoring, logging or a stability workflow, so it provides no sensor data.
9. Rainmeter (https://www.rainmeter.net): Rainmeter shows customizable skins on a Windows desktop, from hardware usage meters to audio visualizers, under GPL v2. Pricing: Free. Rainmeter has been open source software distributed free of charge under the GNU GPL v2 license since February 2001. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It cannot stress-test, tune or diagnose, and meters need a sensor source.
10. Open Hardware Monitor (https://openhardwaremonitor.org/): Open Hardware Monitor is a free open source monitor that runs without installation, but its newest listed release dates from 2020. Pricing: Free and open source; binaries are under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The listed releases stop in 2020, so newer processors and boards may not read correctly.

## Best In-Game Advertising Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-in-game-advertising-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

An in-game advertising platform inserts advertisements into the game itself, for example as billboards, posters or audio spots, and sells that inventory to brands. Unlike full-screen interstitials, native in-game formats aim not to interrupt play. Developers add an SDK, advertisers buy through a platform, and the vendor measures views and clicks.

1. Anzu (https://www.anzu.io/): Covers all three platforms through programmatic buying on standard IAB sizes, which lowers the barrier for advertisers who already buy that way. Pricing: No price is stated on the homepage; advertiser and publisher terms are linked from the site. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No fees, revenue share or minimum traffic are stated on the homepage, and the pages do not describe how ads are placed in a 3D scene.
2. Gadsme (https://www.gadsme.com/): Closest to the native, no-overlay ideal for PC and console, with an SDK that names Unity, Unreal and custom C++ engines. Pricing: No price is stated on the opened pages; visitors are asked to request a demo. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The vendor gives no price and asks for a demo, and the uplift range is its own figure with no named study.
3. Frameplay (https://frameplay.com/): Pairs intrinsic placements with a self-service platform, so smaller advertisers can run campaigns without an agency. Pricing: No price is stated; the homepage offers a Book a demo button. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No pricing is shown, platforms are not listed on the pages we read, and the 33 second figure is the vendor's own average with no stated sample.
4. Adverty (https://adverty.com/): Focuses on in-play placement with viewability measurement and a self-serve portal for both sides. Pricing: No price is stated on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage states no price, supported engines or platforms.
5. Venatus (https://www.venatus.com/): Strong on direct sales and mediation for web and app games, with less visible console specialization. Pricing: No price is stated; the homepage offers a Request demo button. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Its navigation lists websites, apps and browser games, not PC or console titles, so console fit is unconfirmed.
6. Playwire (https://www.playwire.com/): A publisher-side monetization stack with a single mobile SDK, less specific to native in-game formats. Pricing: No price is stated; publishers are asked to apply. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Console is not listed among its surfaces, and the pages describe publisher monetization rather than in-game native placements.
7. Azerion (https://www.azerion.com/): Broad advertising company with a game distribution arm, but its pages talk to advertisers more than to PC and console developers. Pricing: No price is stated; the site asks visitors to get in touch. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No pricing is stated and the pages do not describe native in-game formats or PC and console support.
8. Odeeo (https://odeeo.io/): A different format: audio spots rather than visuals, aimed at mobile, which narrows its use for PC and console readers. Pricing: No price is stated on the page; the site asks visitors to contact the company. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Its pages describe mobile games only, so console and PC studios cannot use it.
9. Kayzen (https://kayzen.io/): Rare in publishing real fees, but it is a demand-side tool for mobile, so it fits readers buying ads, not placing them in PC and console games. Pricing: Starter is $1,250 per month (up to $10,000 ad spend, 15% overage), Pro $5,750 per month (up to $50,000, 13% overage) and Enterprise $15,000 per month (up to $150,000, 10% overage). Free option: None. Falls short: It buys mobile traffic and does not place ads inside game worlds, so a studio looking to earn revenue from PC or console players gets nothing from it.
10. Bigabid (https://www.bigabid.com/user-acquisition/): An acquisition platform for mobile apps with contextual targeting, included as a neighbor to in-game advertising rather than a core member. Pricing: No price is stated on the page; it offers a Let's Get Started button. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: This is not in-game advertising: it acquires users and retargets them.

Influencer marketing tools for games help a studio find streamers and video creators who play its genre, send them review keys, run paid or reward-based campaigns, track coverage and pay creators. Game-specific tools work with keys and storefront data; general creator platforms handle outreach, contracts and reporting across social networks.

1. Keymailer (https://keymailer.co/): First because it is the most direct route from a studio to game creators, with a free creator side, a publisher trial and a security mode. Pricing: Not on the page; no pricing or free plan is shown on the home page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The reach figure is a vendor claim, and the home page shows no prices, platforms or how the verified list is built.

Pricing: Free: $0 per month plus a 20% management fee on wallet deposits. Starter: $200 per month after a 30-day free trial, plus 10%. Growth: $500 per month plus 7%. Scale: $1,500 per month plus 5%. Enterprise: priced with sales. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Examples on the home page come from Uber, Stio and Rookie Wellness, not games, and no game platforms such as Twitch are named.

Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Twitch is not listed, the Shopify focus is built for e-commerce and not for key distribution, and a permanent free plan is not offered.
8. HypeAuditor (https://hypeauditor.com/): Eighth because the vetting and analytics help catch weak audiences and Twitch is covered, but nothing is built around game keys. Pricing: Paid plans, with pricing depending on plan, features and usage limits; exact prices are not on the page. Falls short: Exact paid prices are not shown, and its customers named on the page are retailers such as Notino and MediaMarkt, not game studios.

## Best Live Production Software in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-live-production-software
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Live production software is the control room of a stream. It takes several inputs, such as cameras, screens and remote guests, lets an operator cut between them, adds titles and replays, mixes audio, and outputs one program feed to a platform or server. It can be a program on a computer or a hardware switcher.

1. Wirecast (https://www.wirecast.io/): Wirecast runs on both Mac and Windows, takes unlimited cameras, brings in remote guests and prints its monthly prices. Pricing: Studio is from $34 per month billed yearly ($408 per year) or $59 month to month; Pro is from $42 per month billed yearly. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It is a subscription, so the cost continues every month or year, unlike buying a hardware switcher outright.
2. Blackmagic ATEM (https://www.blackmagicdesign.com/products/atem): Blackmagic's ATEM Constellation line puts dedicated switcher hardware with up to 80 inputs behind a free control application. Pricing: Hardware product; prices are not on the page, and ATEM Software Control is included. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Hardware means a purchase, and prices are not on the page we opened.
3. vMix (https://www.vmix.com/): vMix is a Windows video mixer with instant replay, NDI and SRT inputs and a title designer, with a 60-day trial. Pricing: Homepage shows purchase from $50 per month; a free 60-day trial is offered. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It is Windows only, so Mac-based crews cannot run it.
4. OBS Studio (https://obsproject.com/): OBS Studio costs nothing, runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and composes scenes from webcams, capture cards and browser windows. Pricing: Free and open source software. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The pages we read describe no built-in replay, remote guest feature or vendor support, so you rely on community resources and plugins.
5. Vizrt (https://www.vizrt.com/): Vizrt provides software-defined real-time 3D graphics, live production systems and studio automation for broadcasters. Pricing: Pricing is not stated on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No price appears on the homepage, and the page does not list system requirements or entry-level options.
6. Singular.live (https://www.singular.live/): Singular.live is a web graphics platform for broadcast and esports with a watermarked free tier and an Enterprise plan with SSO. Falls short: It does not switch cameras or encode a stream by itself.
7. NDI Tools (https://ndi.video/tools/): NDI Tools bundles free utilities such as Discovery, Studio Monitor and NDI Free Audio for Windows and macOS. Pricing: Downloadable from the vendor page, which shows no prices. Free option: Free. Falls short: It does not switch, mix or stream anything on its own.
8. Ecamm Live (https://ecamm.com/): Ecamm Live is built for Mac and supports saved scenes, split screens, titles and Stream Deck control. Pricing: Plans are $16 per month (one payment of $192) or $32 per month (one payment of $384), with a 14-day free trial. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It runs only on macOS, so Windows PCs are out.
9. Switcher Studio (https://www.switcherstudio.com/): Switcher Studio is multi-camera live streaming software that sends a stream to several platforms, with a 14-day trial. Falls short: We could not capture the plan amounts, and the pages we read say little about graphics, replay or audio mixing.
10. LiveU Studio (https://www.liveu.tv/): LiveU Studio sits inside a cloud-based, IP-bonded live video lineup for contribution, production and distribution. Pricing: Not stated on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage does not state pricing, and the capabilities of the Studio product are described in one line.
11. Larix Broadcaster (https://softvelum.com/larix/): Larix Broadcaster is a free mobile app for sending video from iOS and Android devices to a server. Pricing: Free. Free option: Free. Falls short: It does not switch, add graphics or produce a show.

## Best Live Streaming APIs and SDKs in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-live-streaming-apis-and-sdks
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A live streaming API is a hosted service that ingests video from an encoder or device, converts it, and delivers it to viewers through code you control. SDKs wrap the same service for web, iOS and Android. They let a product team add live video without building servers, encoders and global delivery themselves.

1. Mux (https://www.mux.com/): Mux prints its live encoding, storage and delivery rates and ships a player and analytics, so a small team can estimate a bill before writing code. Pricing: Pay as you go has no platform fee, with live 1080p Plus encoding at $0.03125 per minute; Launch is $20 per month and Scale is $500 per month. Free option: Free. Falls short: Large-volume pricing is quoted by sales, so very big audiences leave the published rates behind.
2. Amazon IVS (https://aws.amazon.com/ivs/): Amazon IVS is a hosted live service with built-in chat and published hourly rates, a natural fit for interactive streams inside an AWS account. Pricing: Pay as you go from $0.20 per hour for basic channel input, with a first-year free usage tier. Free option: Free. Falls short: The rate card has several line items (input type, output tier, region, participant hours), so estimating a real bill takes some arithmetic.
3. api.video (https://api.video/): api.video gives developers one API for hosting, live streaming, a player and AI transcripts, with free encoding and a free sandbox. Pricing: Pay-as-you-go with free encoding; hosting from $0.00285 per minute stored per month and delivery from $0.0017 per minute delivered. A free sandbox limits videos to 30 seconds with a watermark, deleted after 24 hours. Enterprise is quoted by sales. Free option: Free. Falls short: The sandbox is designed for testing, not for a pilot with real audiences, because clips vanish after a day.
4. LiveKit (https://livekit.com/): LiveKit is an open source framework with a hosted cloud, favored where participants talk back to the stream or an AI agent joins. Pricing: Free account with no credit card, including 1,000 free agent session minutes per month. Paid plans are not listed; custom pricing is available through sales. Free option: Free. Falls short: Public paid plans are not listed; custom pricing runs through sales.
5. Ceeblue (https://www.ceeblue.net/): Ceeblue transcodes and delivers streams in near real time and is one of few here to print monthly euro starting prices. Pricing: Transcoding starts at 375 EUR per month and the Real Time Service Mesh starts at 460 EUR per month. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The entry prices are starting amounts, not full bills, and package prices are not shown.
6. Cloudflare Stream (https://www.cloudflare.com/products/cloudflare-stream/): Cloudflare Stream accepts RTMP and SRT, outputs HLS and DASH, and sits in the same account as many sites' DNS and security. Pricing: The page does not state per-minute prices or a free tier; it describes pricing as simple and predictable and links to a separate pricing page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The product page does not state per-minute prices or a free tier, only a link to a separate pricing page, so we cannot quote rates.
7. 100ms (https://www.100ms.live/): 100ms offers prebuilt rooms plus SDKs for apps that mix broadcast and conversation, such as classes and community events. Pricing: Not stated on the homepage; the page has a Try for Free button and links to a pricing page. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Pricing is not on the homepage, only a link, so we cannot quote it.
8. Agora (https://www.agora.io/en/): Agora combines video and voice calling, interactive live streaming, chat and a conversational AI engine behind SDKs. Pricing: A free tier of 10,000 minutes is offered; paid rates are not stated on the homepage. Free option: Free. Falls short: Paid rates are not on the homepage, so cost planning needs the pricing documentation or sales.
9. Daily (https://www.daily.co/): Daily is a WebRTC platform that maintains the open source Pipecat framework and offers a video SDK with recording and live streaming. Pricing: Free sign-up is offered; the homepage links to separate pricing pages and shows no prices. Free option: Free. Falls short: The homepage lists no prices and points to separate pricing pages for Daily Video and Pipecat Cloud.
10. Twilio (https://www.twilio.com/en-us/video): Twilio Video prices per participant minute and ships SDKs for JavaScript, iOS and Android, aimed at calls more than broadcasts. Pricing: Pay-as-you-go from $0.004 per participant per minute, with volume discounts and no upfront commitment. A free trial needs no credit card. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The page describes calling, not RTMP ingest, HLS output or large-audience live streaming, so it is a poor base for one-to-many events.
11. Vonage (https://www.vonage.com/): Vonage bundles video with voice, messaging and contact center products, which helps buyers who want one telecom vendor. Pricing: The homepage links to pricing pages for communications APIs and unified communications; no prices are on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices appear on the homepage, and the page gives little detail about live streaming, RTMP ingest or audience scale.
12. Dolby OptiView (https://optiview.dolby.com/): Dolby OptiView combines streaming, clipping, ad insertion and a player for providers building fan experiences. Pricing: Pricing is not stated on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing is not stated on the homepage, and nothing there describes a self-serve developer path.
13. Livepeer (https://livepeer.org/): Livepeer now describes itself as an open inference network for AI video jobs, so its current fit is GPU compute more than classic streaming. Falls short: No customer pricing is listed; providers set their own prices.

## Best Mobile Attribution Tools for Games in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-mobile-attribution-tools-for-games
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A mobile attribution tool, often called a mobile measurement partner, matches each install and later in-game event to the ad campaign that drove it. It receives postbacks from ad networks, reads Apple's SKAdNetwork signals on iOS, filters fraud, and reports cost, revenue and retention by channel so a studio can decide where the next marketing dollar goes.

1. AppsFlyer (https://www.appsflyer.com): First because it combines a free starting plan with stated attribution across mobile, web, CTV, PC and console, plus fraud protection. Pricing: Zero plan (free) includes core marketing analytics and a Welcome Package with 12K free conversions for the first year; Growth plan conversions cost $0.07 each after that. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The free allowance covers only the first year, and a per-conversion price rises with every tracked event, so a game with many in-app events can see costs climb quickly.
2. Tenjin (https://tenjin.com): Second because a stated $200 monthly starting plan, free entry and ad monetization reporting fit a small team that wants fewer tools. Pricing: Flexible plans from $200 per month, according to the homepage; free to start with pay-as-you-grow attribution. Free option: Free. Falls short: The platform coverage is not listed on the homepage text we read, so PC and console support is unconfirmed.
3. Airbridge (https://airbridge.io/): Third because the $40+ monthly Core plan, no annual contract and PC and console coverage make it the cheapest published way in. Pricing: Core plan from $40+ per month after a 30-day free trial, with 500K data points included, then $0.0001 per data point; a Growth plan is also offered, with no annual contracts. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The figures on brands and countries are vendor claims, and the pages we read do not describe SKAN setup or deep linking in detail.
4. Singular (https://www.singular.net/): Fourth because its SKAdNetwork, cost aggregation and CTV tools are named plainly, but plan prices are hidden behind a talk-to-us step. Pricing: The pricing page's captured text shows no plan prices; it offers Let's Talk, Book a Demo and Start Free buttons. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Plan prices are absent from the pricing text we read, and what the Start Free button includes is not stated.
5. Kochava (https://kochava.com/): Fifth because it offers a free tier and marketing mix modeling, with Huawei coverage, while hiding every price figure. Pricing: The home page shows a free tier called Free App Analytics and a Compare Plans and Pricing link, with no specific prices; marketing mix modeling is priced by ad spend volume and number of unique models. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: No concrete prices appear on the page, including for the paid plans behind the Compare Plans link, and what the free tier excludes is not spelled out.
6. Branch (https://branch.io/): Sixth because its journey-linking strength suits web-to-app flows, yet its customers are mostly non-gaming and no price appears. Pricing: No prices shown on the home page; it links to a Pricing section that was not opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No customer on the home page is a game company, no price or free plan is shown, and Android is not explicitly named in the text we read.
7. Affise (https://www.affise.com/): Seventh because its attribution product is secondary to affiliate tracking, and the printed prices apply to the latter. Pricing: Affise Performance plans run from $499 per month on yearly billing ($625 monthly) with a 14-day trial; the mobile attribution product is sold through Talk to an expert and is not priced in the opened text. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The printed prices are for the affiliate product, not the mobile attribution one, and its homepage text does not detail SKAN, PC or console coverage.
8. Apple Search Ads (https://ads.apple.com/app-store/): Eighth because it is an ad channel with its own attribution rather than a neutral measurement partner, though the Attribution API helps. Pricing: Cost-per-tap pricing; set-price amounts are not on the page. Eligible developers who sign up get a 100 USD credit, subject to terms and conditions. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It measures only its own channel and cannot compare Apple against other networks.
9. Kayzen (https://kayzen.io/): Ninth because it is a buying platform with published plan prices rather than an independent attribution tool. Pricing: Starter $1,250 per month (up to $10,000 ad spend, 15% overage), Pro $5,750 per month (up to $50,000, 13% overage), Enterprise $15,000 per month (up to $150,000, 10% overage). Free option: None. Falls short: It buys media; it does not provide neutral attribution, so you still need a measurement partner to judge results.
10. Moloco (https://www.moloco.com/): Tenth because it is an advertising engine with performance pricing, not a measurement tool, and shows few specifics. Pricing: Moloco Ads uses performance-based campaign pricing; overall pricing depends on product, campaign goals, market and level of advertising activity. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The page does not state a founding year, headquarters or ownership, and gives no price figures.

A mobile game ad network buys and sells advertising inside apps, while a mediation platform sits above several networks and runs an auction so each ad slot goes to the highest bidder. Rewarded video, where players choose to watch an ad for an in-game reward, is the format most mobile games build around.

Falls short: The page names no fee, revenue share or list of connected networks, so you cannot see cost or demand depth before signing up.

Falls short: The page does not list fees or revenue share.

URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-mod-managers-for-pc-games
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A mod manager is a desktop program that downloads, installs, enables and orders community modifications for a game, usually without overwriting the original files. Good ones handle load order, conflicts and updates. Some tie to one mod site, some cover hundreds of games, and some automate whole modlists.

1. Vortex (https://github.com/Nexus-Mods/Vortex): It covers over 250 games, sorts load orders and is free under GPL-3.0, which makes it the widest general-purpose pick here. Pricing: Free and open source under GPL-3.0. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The README did not list supported operating systems in the text we read, and it ties you closely to the Nexus ecosystem.
2. Mod Organizer 2 (https://modorganizer2.org/): Profiles, load order tools, a virtual file system and conflict handling, free and open source on Windows. Pricing: Free and open source. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It is Windows only per the vendor, and its profile model has a steeper learning curve than a one-click app.
3. r2modman (https://thunderstore.io/c/riskofrain2/p/ebkr/r2modman/): A simple manager for games distributed through Thunderstore, with 10.8M downloads on its listing. Pricing: No price is shown on the Thunderstore listing; the source is on GitHub. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It works for Thunderstore games only, and the listing shows no price or platform list.
4. Thunderstore (https://thunderstore.io/): A mod database claiming over 110,000 mods across 300+ games, with a Windows mod manager and an API. Pricing: No pricing is shown on the home page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The home page shows no pricing or free-plan details.
5. Wabbajack (https://www.wabbajack.org/): Installs an entire curated modlist automatically, free and open source under GPL3. Pricing: Free and open source. The repository links a GPL3 LICENSE.txt file. Free option: Open source. Falls short: It installs lists rather than managing individual mods day to day, and the pages do not name supported games or operating systems.
6. CurseForge (https://curseforge.com/): A mod platform with a free client, one-click installs and games such as Minecraft, World of Warcraft and The Sims 4. Pricing: Free client; CurseForge Premium is an ad-free upgrade with no price on the page. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Premium pricing is not on the page, and the mod and download counts, such as 620K+ mods and 150B+ downloads, are vendor claims.
7. Modrinth (https://modrinth.com/): An open-source platform for Minecraft content with a desktop app, Fabric, Forge and NeoForge loaders and creator revenue. Pricing: Not shown on the page; it links to Modrinth+, Modrinth App and Modrinth Hosting with no prices. Creators can earn ad revenue from project pages. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It covers Minecraft only, and the page shows no prices for Modrinth+ or Hosting.
8. Prism Launcher (https://prismlauncher.org/): Manages multiple Minecraft instances with one-click mod loader installs and modpack imports. Pricing: Free; the project accepts donations and publishes under open-source licenses. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Minecraft only, and it states it is not affiliated with Mojang or Microsoft.

## Best Multiplayer Networking SDKs in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-multiplayer-networking-sdks
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A multiplayer networking SDK is the library or service that moves game state between players: it synchronizes objects, manages rooms or sessions, handles connections and often hosts relay or server infrastructure. Studios pick one per engine, then layer matchmaking, voice and persistence on top.

1. Photon (https://photonengine.com/): The widest bundle here: Fusion, Quantum, rooms, voice, chat and a hosted cloud, with the vendor claiming a very large player base. Pricing: Not published on the homepage; a Try Photon free sign-up and mentions of pricing plans without figures. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The homepage shows no prices and talks only of cost-effective plans, so you must sign up to see limits.
2. Mirror (https://mirror-networking.com/): A long-standing open source Unity library with source on GitHub and docs on GitBook, simple to evaluate and free to start. Pricing: No price on the page; Mirror is open source with a Unity Asset Store download and no license name stated. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The homepage names no license, no price, no feature list and no supported platforms beyond Unity, so evaluation means reading the repository.
3. Fish-Networking (https://fish-networking.gitbook.io/): A free Unity solution with a server-authoritative design, dedicated-server or host mode and explicit no-cap terms. Pricing: Free, with no CCU caps or CCU paywalls according to the documentation. Free option: Free. Falls short: Unity only, and the documentation site does not mention hosted infrastructure, voice or matchmaking, so those come from other tools.
4. Netcode for GameObjects (https://unity.com/products/netcode): First-party Unity netcode aimed at casual co-op, with a Distributed Authority mode and linked Matchmaker, sessions and voice services. Pricing: No price on the page; it links a View pricing page for Unity gaming services. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices appear on this page, and platform support is described only as 25+ without names.
5. Colyseus (https://colyseus.io/): The most engine-flexible pick, MIT licensed with built-in matchmaking, state sync and a priced managed cloud. Pricing: Framework is MIT licensed and free; Colyseus Cloud starts at $15 per month. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Several client SDKs are marked alpha, so Godot, GameMaker and C support carries risk.
6. Normcore (https://normcore.io/): Automatic sync, voice, networked physics and global hosting for Unity, sold with usage-based billing and a sales path for private clouds. Pricing: Start for free, then pay for what you use with no hidden fees or CCU caps; plan prices not stated. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: Plan prices are not shown, only a Contact Sales button.
7. coherence (https://coherence.io/): Pairs a Unity multiplayer engine with hosting you can run on cloud, peer-to-peer, self-managed or hybrid setups. Pricing: A Start for free button, but no plan prices; the pricing FAQ answer is not visible on the homepage. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The page hides its cost answer, and no prices are shown.
8. SpacetimeDB (https://spacetimedb.com/): Treats the database as the game server, with reducers, subscriptions and built-in auth, suiting state-heavy designs. Pricing: No pricing terms on the homepage; a pricing page is linked. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It is not a netcode library in the usual sense, so physics-heavy action games must adapt.
9. Nakama (https://heroiclabs.com/): An open source server for social multiplayer features that doubles as a backend, but it is more a platform than a netcode library. Pricing: Open source download offered; homepage names no license or price. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The homepage does not name a license.
10. Unity Gaming Services (https://unity.com/solutions/gaming-services): Live features such as Cloud Code and Authentication, though this page lists no netcode and does not mention Multiplay or Matchmaker. Pricing: Get started for free and a View Pricing link; no figures on the page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: This page lists no networking product, so it cannot be your netcode choice.

## Best Multistreaming Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-multistreaming-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A multistreaming platform takes one live video signal, from a camera, an encoder or a browser studio, and relays it to several destinations at the same moment, such as YouTube, Facebook, Twitch, LinkedIn or a custom RTMP address. It saves running separate encoders and often adds chat merging, scheduling and recording.

1. OneStream Live (https://onestream.live/): The most documented plan ladder in this group, with a usable free tier and several ways to feed it a signal. Pricing: Free at $0 forever (2 destinations, 720p, 1 GB storage); Basic $15 per month, Standard $39, Professional $49, Enterprise $99, with lower yearly rates. The pricing page does not name the currency. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The pricing page prints dollar signs without naming a currency, so finance teams should confirm it at checkout.
2. Castr (https://castr.com/): Pairs relay to social destinations with its own hosted delivery, so one vendor covers both the broadcast and the website embed. Pricing: Five plans from $16.67 per month, with a 7-day trial on the Starter plan. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: There is no permanent free plan, only the trial.
3. Livepush (https://livepush.io/): Strong on unattended channels: scheduling, playlists, looping and a branded player in one cloud service. Pricing: Free plan with 20 streaming hours a month and no card required; paid plans from $13 per month billed yearly ($15 billed monthly), according to the FAQ. Tier prices are not listed per tier. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The page names tiers (Creators, Business, Studio, Enterprise) but gives one starting price rather than a price per tier, so the real cost of a larger plan is unclear.
4. Restream (https://restream.io/): A familiar, browser-first starting point, held back here only by what its pages let us confirm. Pricing: The pricing page says to start multistreaming for free or choose a plan; plan prices were not captured from the page we read. Free option: Free. Falls short: We could not record plan prices, destination limits or resolution caps from the opened pages, so any buyer has to check the pricing page directly.
5. Streamster (https://streamster.io/): The only tool here with a per-hour pay-as-you-go option, which fits a company that streams a handful of launches a year. Pricing: FREE $0 (2 channels, 720p/30); LITE $15 per month (4 channels); REGULAR $30 (6 channels, transcoding); PROFESSIONAL $50 (8 channels, 2K/60); PREMIUM $75 (10 channels, 4K/60); pay-per-use from $0.48 to $1.92 per hour. Currency not named; no annual plans. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: No annual discount is shown, so a team streaming weekly pays full monthly rates.
6. Lightstream (https://golightstream.com/): Good for game-event streams that start on a console, but capped at five destinations. Pricing: Free tier at $0 (Lightstream logo, 720p, 10 hours per stream, 3 scenes); Premium $12 per month or $9 per month on an annual plan (no logo, 1080p, 48 hours, 20 scenes). Free option: Free. Falls short: The five-destination cap is the lowest ceiling among paid tools that publish one, and the free tier burns a Lightstream logo into every stream.
7. Be.Live (https://be.live/): Audience-interaction extras are the draw; the missing price on its home page is the drawback. Pricing: Not published on the home page we opened; the page shows promotional banners and a 14-day free trial with no credit card. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The home page prints discount banners (50%, 25%, 33%) but no list prices, and we did not open the packages page, so cost is the biggest unknown.
8. Riverside (https://riverside.com/): Best when the stream doubles as a recording session; its multistream role is a side feature. Pricing: Free plan at $0 (720p, watermark, 2 hours of multi-track recording); Pro billed $288 annually (up to 4K, no watermark); Business priced separately. The pricing page carried a staging notice and may not be current. Free option: Free plan. Falls short: The multistream features are described in less depth than its recording features on the pages we read, so destination counts are unknown.
9. OBS Studio (https://obsproject.com/): The production layer many relay services expect, free to use, but it does not relay to many destinations by itself. Pricing: Free and open source software. Free option: Open source. Falls short: By itself it sends a single outgoing stream, so reaching several platforms needs a relay service or extra plugins that the pages we read do not describe.
10. Prism Live Studio (https://prismlive.com/en_us/): A no-cost desktop studio with a phone companion, aimed at creators rather than business teams. Pricing: The desktop app is free; a Plus subscription and Credits are sold only in the PRISM mobile app. Free option: Free. Falls short: Plus and Credits can only be bought inside the mobile app, which is awkward for company purchasing.
11. Streamlabs Desktop (https://streamlabs.com/): A creator toolkit first; business multistream needs are not documented in what we could read. Pricing: Plans were not recorded: the product page is rendered by JavaScript. The pricing page says the company takes zero cut of donations. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The Desktop product page could not be read in full, so plans, destination limits and platform support are unrecorded here.
12. Larix Broadcaster (https://softvelum.com/larix/): A contribution tool for phones, not a multistream service, so it ends the list. Pricing: Free. Free option: Free. Falls short: The pages we read list only two features, mobile streaming and remote contribution, and say nothing about sending one stream to several destinations.

## Best Open-Source Game Engines in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-open-source-game-engines
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

An open-source game engine is one whose source code is published under a license that lets you use, study and often modify it, usually without fees or royalties. The terms differ: MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0 and zlib are permissive, while source-available licenses restrict some uses. This list covers engines and libraries for 2D, 3D and the web.

1. Godot (https://godotengine.org/): Community governance through the Godot Foundation and a long sponsor list make it the safest open-source default. Pricing: Nothing to pay. Described as a free, open-source engine; the homepage does not state which license applies. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The license name does not appear in the homepage text, so you must check the repository for exact terms.
2. Bevy (https://bevy.org/): A permissive dual license, a published donor ladder and a clear no-sales-cut statement give it the cleanest terms here. Pricing: Free of contracts, license fees and sales cuts. Monthly donor tiers exist from $25 up to $6,000. Free option: Open source. Falls short: There is no foundation named on the homepage, so long-term stewardship rests on donors and contributors.
3. Stride (https://stride3d.net/): MIT terms that explicitly cover both editor and runtime, plus a named foundation sponsor, for the C# community. Pricing: Free. Editor and runtime sources carry the MIT license, per the homepage, and a donation page on Open Collective is linked. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Named targets are desktop and VR only, so mobile and console plans lack confirmation.
4. O3DE (https://o3de.org/): Neutral governance under the Open 3D Foundation is the draw; license wording is missing from the homepage. Pricing: No price stated. The page promotes donations and Become a Member; the license is not named in the text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The software license is not named on the homepage, which is an odd omission for an open-source page, and no platform list is given.
5. Phaser (https://github.com/phaserjs/phaser): MIT licensing plus a company, Phaser Studio Inc, that develops it with the community for more than 13 years. Pricing: Free under MIT, as stated on the official repository page. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Company involvement means roadmap decisions rest partly with Phaser Studio, which some purists treat as a dependency.
6. Solar2D (https://solar2d.com/): A transparent MIT license and a story of surviving a vendor's exit, funded by user sponsors. Pricing: Free under MIT with no hidden fees, charges or royalties, per the homepage. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Funding depends on user sponsorship, so continuity risk is higher than for foundation-hosted projects.
7. LOVE (https://love2d.org/): One of the most liberal licenses on the page, proven by a hit game, though governance details are thin. Pricing: Costs nothing and can be used commercially without limitations under the zlib/libpng license. Free option: Open source. Falls short: No governing body or contributor policy appears on the homepage.
8. Excalibur.js (https://excaliburjs.com/): A short permissive BSD license with an optional paid support page, written entirely in TypeScript. Pricing: Free under the BSD 2 Clause license; the Premium Support page shows no price. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The facts do not show a foundation or a count of contributors.
9. raylib (https://raylib.com/): A plain-C library with grant history, backed by awards, but its homepage skips the license name. Pricing: Free and open source, with donations through GitHub Sponsors, Patreon and Ko-fi; the license name is not in the page text. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The license is not named on the homepage text, which weakens a ranking built around licenses.
10. KAPLAY (https://kaplayjs.com/): A friendly web library with named sponsors, but with no license name on its homepage. Pricing: Free; the homepage says it is open source and always will be, with optional donations on Open Collective and Cafecito. Free option: Open source. Falls short: The homepage names no license and gives no governance model.
11. Babylon.js (https://www.babylonjs.com/): A feature-heavy open web renderer whose homepage gives no license, ranked low on that criterion alone. Pricing: The homepage states neither a price nor a license. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No license, no pricing and no governance model appear on the homepage.
12. Three.js (https://threejs.org/): The least documented entry: a title, a release link and a repository, with no license named on the page. Pricing: The homepage states neither price nor license. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Nothing on the homepage identifies the license, the maintainers' governance or any funding route.

## Best PC Benchmarking Software in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-pc-benchmarking-software
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

PC benchmarking software runs a repeatable workload, or records a real game session, and turns the result into numbers you can compare: scores for a CPU or graphics card, frame times for a running game, read and write speeds for a drive. Studios use it to set minimum specs; players use it to check an upgrade or chase a stutter.

1. CapFrameX (https://www.capframex.com/): CapFrameX records and plots frame times from real play, builds on PresentMon, and costs nothing to download. Pricing: Free download. The download page offers an installer and a portable version as .zip files; the homepage also links a Donate page. Free option: Free. Falls short: It runs on Windows only and requires the .NET 10.0 Desktop Runtime.
2. 3DMark (https://www.3dmark.com/): 3DMark from UL Solutions tests gaming performance on PCs, handhelds and phones, and compares results online for $34.99. Pricing: For Windows $34.99; For macOS $34.99; For Windows and macOS $34.99, sold through UL Solutions, Steam and Epic Games; iOS and Android apps are free; the demo can be tried first. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: A score does not reveal stutter inside a particular game.
3. PresentMon (https://github.com/GameTechDev/PresentMon): PresentMon is Intel's open tool set that traces CPU, GPU and display frame durations across DirectX, OpenGL and Vulkan on Windows. Pricing: Pricing is not stated on the repository page. The source is published on GitHub with a LICENSE.txt file in the repository. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It is aimed at developers: the pages we read describe capture tools, not a friendly results browser, and state no price.
4. Cinebench (https://www.maxon.net/en/cinebench): Cinebench 2026 uses the Redshift rendering engine to measure CPU and GPU performance, and Maxon offers it as a download. Pricing: Download offered on the vendor page; no price is stated on the opened page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The page shows no price or license text in our facts, no platform list was captured, and the workload is a render, not a game.
5. NVIDIA FrameView (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/technologies/frameview/): FrameView is NVIDIA's free app that records FPS, frame times, GPU power and performance per watt. Pricing: Free. The vendor page describes it as the free FrameView app. Free option: Free. Falls short: The pages we read do not list supported operating systems, and the tool offers no cross-machine score database.
6. Unigine Superposition (https://benchmark.unigine.com/superposition): Superposition is a free Windows and Linux stress and performance test with a loop mode, VR mode and leaderboards. Pricing: Free download; commercial licenses are listed at $19.95, $495 and $7500 (tax not included), with license types for VR users, hardware manufacturers and commercial companies. Free option: Free. Falls short: Commercial use is licensed separately, with listed prices of $19.95, $495 and $7500 before tax.
7. FurMark (https://geeks3d.com/furmark/): FurMark 2 loads a GPU very hard on Windows and Linux and doubles as an OpenGL and Vulkan benchmark with online scores. Pricing: Free. The vendor page says FurMark is simple to use and is free. Free option: Free. Falls short: A stress test pushes loads no game reaches, so temperatures and power can look worse than real use.
8. AIDA64 (https://www.aida64.com): AIDA64 from FinalWire combines hardware detection, sensor monitoring, stress and benchmark tests, sold as editions with a product key. Pricing: Pricing is not shown on the opened pages. AIDA64 is licensed with a product key; the licensing page describes support and maintenance periods, renewals, and trial versions. Editions are Extreme, Engineer, Business and Network Audit. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No prices appear on the pages we read, only license terms with a product key and renewable maintenance periods.
9. PCMark 10 (https://benchmarks.ul.com/pcmark10): PCMark 10 benchmarks office PCs in Express and Professional editions, but UL is steering new buyers toward Procyon. Pricing: Editions include PCMark 10 Express and Professional Edition; exact prices are not shown on the opened page. The vendor says it is encouraging new customers to choose Procyon. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Exact prices are not shown on the opened page.
10. UserBenchmark (https://www.userbenchmark.com): UserBenchmark runs a one-minute speed test and ranks CPUs, GPUs, SSDs, HDDs, RAM and USB devices from user data. Pricing: Free. The homepage offers a free speed test and a free download. Free option: Free. Falls short: Results come from a user-driven database rather than a controlled workload, so they vary with background software.

## Best Pixel Streaming and Cloud Game Streaming Platforms for Studios in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-pixel-streaming-and-cloud-game-streaming-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Pixel streaming runs a game or real-time 3D application on a GPU server and sends the rendered video to a browser or device, so viewers need no download or powerful hardware. Studios use it for playable demos, product configurators, trade-show builds and cloud game launches. Platforms differ in engine support, billing and how much infrastructure you operate yourself.

1. Eagle 3D Streaming (https://www.eagle3dstreaming.com/): It streams Unreal Engine 5 apps to any browser, needs no end-user GPU and offers a free trial with no credit card. Pricing: Free trial with no credit card; a plan starts free before scaling with Core, and annual billing includes 2 free months. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: The pricing amounts for the Core plan were not in the text we read, the company and country were not captured, and the pages stress Unreal Engine 5 rather than Unity or other engines.
2. Streampixel (https://www.streampixel.io/): One flat EUR 99 monthly plan with unlimited minutes and 2 concurrent users, plus a 2-day free trial. Pricing: EUR 99 per month with unlimited minutes and 2 concurrent users; EUR 45 per month per extra concurrent user; 2-day free trial. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Concurrency is the constraint: 2 sessions are included, so a busy launch costs more.
3. PureWeb (https://www.pureweb.com/): It names both Unreal Engine and Unity and offers Pixel Streaming and Render Streaming for browser delivery. Pricing: Not stated in the extracted text of the home page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No pricing appeared in the text of the home page, and no company, country or trial terms were captured.
4. Amazon GameLift Streams (https://aws.amazon.com/gamelift/streams/): A managed streaming service on AWS, useful if your team already holds an AWS account and billing relationship. Pricing: The overview page has a Pricing section and links to AWS Pricing; plan amounts are not in the extracted text. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The extracted page was mostly AWS navigation, so features and prices could not be read in detail.
5. Vagon (https://vagon.io/): A browser-based cloud computer billed by the minute, with app streaming and team management. Pricing: Billed by the minute from $0.25/hr, with a $7.99/mo monthly fee listed; a trial with 1 hour is listed at $0.99. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It is a cloud computer first, so session management for many anonymous viewers is not its focus.
6. Ubitus (https://ubitus.ai/): An established cloud gaming company with GPU virtualization and a cloud streaming platform, aimed at business customers. Pricing: No prices are shown on the pages opened; the site presents enterprise and business solutions. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices are shown, and the site presents enterprise solutions, so a small studio should expect a sales process.
7. Edgegap (https://edgegap.com/): Per-minute game server hosting across many locations, with cloud gaming named among its use cases. Pricing: Pay per minute on edge cloud with no upfront costs or fixed monthly fees. No specific prices on the homepage; a pricing calculator is linked. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It is not a turnkey pixel streaming product, and no specific prices appear on the homepage.
8. Paperspace (https://paperspace.com): A cloud GPU platform billed per second, with cloud desktops, notebooks and a full API for teams that assemble their own pipeline. Pricing: Exact prices not shown on the homepage; it states low-cost GPUs with per-second billing and savings of up to 70% on compute costs. Free option: Free. Falls short: The homepage is AI-focused and shows no exact prices.
9. CoreWeave (https://coreweave.com/): GPU and CPU compute, storage and managed Kubernetes with published hourly rates, though aimed at AI workloads. Pricing: The pricing page lists on-demand GPU instance prices per hour (for example $42.00 per hour for one listed configuration, and spot prices for others); several rows say Contact sales. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Nothing on the pages we read is aimed at game streaming, so a studio would have to build session management, deployment and the browser client.
10. Shadow (https://shadow.tech/eu/): A full Windows PC in the cloud launched from a browser, handy for private demos but not built for public streams. Pricing: Not stated in the extracted text of the opened pages. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Plan prices were not in the readable text, and nothing describes multi-viewer session handling, embedding or analytics.

## Best Player Support Software for Games in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-player-support-software-for-games
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Player support software is a help desk or messaging tool adapted to games: players open a ticket from inside the game, a bot or an agent answers in their language, and the studio sees volume by topic. It differs from generic customer service tools by SDKs for mobile and PC, console handoff and community links.

1. Helpshift (https://helpshift.com/): Helpshift comes first because it pairs in-game support SDKs and console handoff with named game-studio case studies. Pricing: Not on page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices are published, so the first budget figure comes from sales.
2. AIHelp (https://aihelp.net/): AIHelp ranks second as a support platform with a mobile SDK, web chat, AI bots and a free trial offer. Pricing: A 'Get Free Trial' offer; pricing details are on a separate Pricing page that was not opened. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Pricing sits on a separate page that we did not open, and the home page gives no plan amounts.
3. Zendesk (https://www.zendesk.com/): Zendesk takes third place for studios that want mature ticketing, a knowledge base and an app marketplace. Pricing: 14 days free trial, no credit card required; eligible startups can get up to 2 years free; plan prices are not on the page, which links to plans and pricing. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Plan prices are not on the home page, and nothing in what we read describes an in-game SDK or console handoff, so a studio needs extra work to connect it to the client.
4. Intercom (https://intercom.com/): It sits fourth because it publishes a seat price and outcome fee, giving studios a bill they can model. Pricing: Helpdesk with Fin AI Agent: $19 per seat per month plus $0.99 per outcome; spending limits can be set; 14 day free trial with no credit card required; no free plan mentioned. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Outcome fees can climb during a launch spike, which is why spending limits matter.
5. Kustomer (https://kustomer.com/): Kustomer ranks fifth as an omnichannel platform whose CRM keeps player history in one timeline. Pricing: Not on page; a Pricing link exists but no prices or free-plan details are shown. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: A pricing link exists but no prices or free plan appear.
6. Ada (https://ada.cx/): Ada places sixth since it centers on automated resolution across channels rather than a full help desk. Pricing: Not on page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Prices are not published, the claimed resolution rate is vendor-reported, and no game customers or console handoff are named.
7. Trengo (https://trengo.com/): Trengo lands seventh as a shared inbox that gathers WhatsApp, email, chat and social messages for small teams. Pricing: Pricing page linked from the homepage (/prices); no amounts shown on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing page is linked but amounts are not shown on the home page.
8. Crisp (https://crisp.chat/): Crisp comes eighth as a compact helpdesk with chat, inbox and knowledge base from a French company. Pricing: The homepage links to a pricing page (/en/pricing/); no amounts shown on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing page is linked, but the home page shows no amounts.
9. Front (https://front.com/): Front takes ninth because it treats support as a shared inbox with ticketing and AI copilots for email-first teams. Pricing: The homepage links to a pricing page (front.com/pricing); no amounts shown on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices appear on the home page, only a link to a pricing page.
10. LiveChat (https://livechat.com/): LiveChat ranks tenth because it is website chat with stated per-user pricing, not a game-focused tool. Pricing: The homepage says pricing starts from $19 per user per month; the pricing page is at /pricing/ and was not opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing page was not opened, so extra plan limits are unknown.
11. Tidio (https://tidio.com/): Tidio sits eleventh since it offers a low-cost entry plan, but it was built for online stores. Pricing: The homepage says paid plans start at $29/mo and links to Contact sales and registration; the pricing page (tidio.com/pricing) was not opened. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The pricing page was not opened, so tier limits are unknown.
12. Sprinklr (https://sprinklr.com/): Sprinklr is twelfth as an enterprise suite that suits large publishers but is heavy for most studios. Pricing: No prices listed on the homepage; it links to Contact Us and Demo pages. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing is quote-only, with contact and demo links instead of amounts.
13. Sendbird (https://sendbird.com/): Sendbird takes thirteenth since it is an API and AI concierge for enterprises, with little stated about games. Pricing: No pricing visible on the homepage. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The home page names no customers, headquarters or founding year, and no pricing is visible.
14. Discord (https://discord.com/): Discord ends the list because it is a community chat app, not a ticketing system. Pricing: No prices on the homepage; it links to a Nitro page (discord.com/nitro). Free option: Unknown. Falls short: It does not provide ticket queues, SLAs or per-player history in what we read, and no prices appear on the home page beyond a link to Nitro.

## Best Playtesting Platforms in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-playtesting-platforms
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

Playtesting platforms let a studio get real players to try an unfinished game and report what happened. Some recruit testers and record sessions for analysis, some only deliver builds through a store or beta channel, and general research tools run moderated or unmoderated sessions that a team can adapt to games.

1. PlaytestCloud (https://playtestcloud.com/): Built for games: recruits a player panel, records sessions and analyzes them, with a free trial of two players. Pricing: No plan prices or per-tester rates are shown; a free trial lets you watch two players for up to 30 minutes, and the page mentions special pricing for small studios. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No plan prices or per-tester rates are published on the page we opened, and console is not listed.
2. Steam Playtest (https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/features/playtest): A no-cost way to put a build in front of real Steam users, with limited or open signup and key controls. Pricing: Valve says Steam Playtest is completely free for customers and developers; charging for access is prohibited and keys may not be sold. Free option: Free. Falls short: It supplies testers and a delivery channel, not recordings, surveys or analysis: you must collect feedback yourself.
3. Lookback (https://www.lookback.com/): General research tool with clear yearly prices, usable for moderated game interviews that you recruit yourself. Pricing: Lookback lists Freelance at $299 a year, Team at $1,782 a year, Insights Hub at $4,122 a year and Enterprise on request, with a trial of 5 free sessions for 60 days. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Nothing on the opened pages mentions games, game engines or built-in player recruitment beyond one panel participant on Freelance.
4. TestFlight (https://developer.apple.com/testflight/): Distributes builds to up to 10,000 external testers on Apple platforms, with built-in feedback. Pricing: The opened page makes no statement about whether TestFlight costs money. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Apple platforms only, and the page does not state a price or describe recorded sessions.
5. Firebase App Distribution (https://firebase.google.com/products/app-distribution): Sends builds to testers on iOS and Android from the console, CI servers or an API, at no cost. Pricing: The page calls App Distribution a no cost tool within the Firebase platform and mentions no usage limits. Free option: Free. Falls short: The page does not mention Unity or Flutter, and it has no player panel, video recording or survey tool.
6. Userlytics (https://www.userlytics.com/): Runs moderated, unmoderated and AI-moderated studies on apps and prototypes with a global panel. Pricing: The pricing page offers pay-per-session or subscription across Project-based, Enterprise, Self-recruitment, Limitless and Custom plans; prices are not shown in the text we opened. ## Best Streaming Media Servers in 2026
URL: https://ga-forum.com/software/best-streaming-media-servers
Last reviewed: 2026-11-18

A streaming media server is software that accepts live video from a camera or encoder, converts it when needed, and serves it to viewers in formats such as HLS or WebRTC. You can run it on your own machines or rent it as a managed service. It sits between the encoder and the audience.

1. Ant Media Server (https://antmedia.io/): Ant Media Server speaks WebRTC, HLS, RTMP and SRT, ships mobile and web SDKs, and lists its instance prices openly. Pricing: Flex is $0.35 per instance-hour; the monthly plan has a regular price of $129 per instance, with a 14-day free trial on Enterprise Edition. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: It is a commercial product, so you pay per instance even when your audience is small; the open source servers below cost nothing in licenses.
2. OvenMediaEngine (https://ovenmedia.com/ome.html): OvenMediaEngine from OvenMedia Labs ships as community software, an Enterprise edition and a managed cloud, so you can start free and buy support later. Pricing: Not captured; the page lists a source and community edition, an Enterprise edition and OvenMedia Cloud without prices. Free option: Open source. Falls short: No price amounts appear on the page we opened, and it does not list protocol support in the text we captured, so check the documentation for WebRTC, SRT and LL-HLS details.
3. SRS (https://ossrs.io/): SRS is an open source server for RTMP, WebRTC, HLS, HTTP-FLV, SRT and MPEG-DASH, packaged for Docker and Kubernetes. Pricing: Free open source project; the vendor page links to its GitHub and license information. Free option: Open source. Falls short: Support comes from a community, not a contract, so you carry the operational risk.
4. Wowza (https://www.wowza.com): Wowza's Streaming Engine runs in a data center, a cloud, at the edge or fully disconnected, with a REST API for automation. Pricing: The pricing page offers a trial and premium support plans; no price amounts appear in the pages we opened. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: No price amounts appear on the pages we opened, only a trial and premium support plans, so budgeting needs a quote.
5. MediaMTX (https://github.com/bluenviron/mediamtx): MediaMTX reads, publishes, proxies, records and plays back streams across SRT, WebRTC, RTSP, RTMP, LL-HLS and more. Pricing: Distributed via the public GitHub repository; we opened no vendor pricing page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: We opened the GitHub repository only, not a pricing or license page, so confirm license terms yourself.
6. Red5 (https://www.red5.net/): Red5 offers an open source media server and the licensed Red5 Pro and Red5 Cloud, with a 30-day free trial advertised. Pricing: Red5 Pro offers monthly or annual subscriptions for developers, startups, SMEs and enterprises; Red5 Cloud has separate pricing. The homepage advertises a 30-day free trial. Free option: Free trial. Falls short: Subscription amounts are not in the text we captured, so you need the pricing page.
7. Nimble Streamer (https://softvelum.com/nimble/): Nimble Streamer supports SRT, RTMP, WebRTC with WHIP ingest, NDI, SDI and Apple Low Latency HLS, with transcoding as a paid add-on. Pricing: Not captured: the pricing page address returned a 404, and the homepage lists no prices. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing is unclear: the pricing page address we tried returned a 404 and the homepage lists no amounts.
8. mediasoup (https://mediasoup.org/): mediasoup is a library, not a ready server: it runs as a Node.js module or Rust crate under the ISC License. Pricing: Free to use under the ISC License (per the license page). Free option: Open source. Falls short: It is not an out-of-the-box RTMP or HLS server, so ingesting broadcast encoders needs extra components.
9. Janus (https://janus.conf.meetecho.com/): Janus is a WebRTC server from Meetecho whose features come from server-side plugins that browsers contact through it. Pricing: Not stated on the page. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: Pricing, license and supported protocols are not stated on the page we read, and no commercial support option appeared.
10. Flussonic (https://flussonic.com/): Flussonic builds streaming software around its Media Server for ingest, transcoding, DVR and delivery, aimed at IPTV, OTT and surveillance. Pricing: Not stated on the homepage; the vendor asks visitors to contact sales. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices are shown and the page links to contact pages.
11. AWS Elemental MediaLive (https://aws.amazon.com/medialive/): AWS Elemental MediaLive encodes live video in the AWS cloud for 24/7 linear channels and live events. Pricing: Not captured; the page links to AWS pricing pages for MediaLive without listing prices. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: The page we opened does not list prices, only a link to AWS pricing pages, so cost modeling needs more reading.
12. Unified Streaming (https://www.unified-streaming.com/): Unified Streaming sells software for live and VOD packaging, live-to-VOD and audio, with licenses issued through a license manager. Pricing: Not stated on the homepage; licenses are managed through a license manager and the vendor offers a demo. Free option: Unknown. Falls short: No prices or protocol details are stated on the page we opened, and the offer is aimed at operators with an existing pipeline.
